articles.title: GBP/USD Reversal Test: Can UK CPI Sustain BoE Tightening Bets Beyond November? - Action Forex
articles.summary: GBP/USD Reversal Test: Can UK CPI Sustain BoE Tightening Bets Beyond November?  Action Forex
articles.full_text:
TL;DR: A November BoE hike is 93.2% priced, but economists are far less convinced about what follows—with this week’s UK wages and September CPI data set to decide whether December tightening gets closer to certainty, just as GBP/USD tests the key 1.3341 Fibonacci resistance.
Why This Matters
Financial markets are preparing for a Bank of England tightening cycle extending well into 2027, but economists are considerably less convinced about what follows November. A 25bps increase next month is already 93.2% priced, while expectations for further hikes depend on evidence that inflation pressures are spreading beyond energy costs. This week’s UK wages and CPI data could determine whether markets are getting ahead of the evidence or correctly anticipating a more persistent inflation problem.
Meanwhile, GBP/USD is testing the 1.3341 Fibonacci resistance following its rebound from 1.3135. With much of the recovery driven by Dollar weakness, Sterling may need more than confirmation of November’s widely anticipated hike to sustain further gains. The critical question is whether incoming UK data reinforce expectations for another increase as early as December, or support Governor Andrew Bailey’s more cautious assessment of second-round inflation pressures.
November Hike Nearly Priced, but Markets Expect Much More
Interest rate markets have moved beyond debating whether the BoE will raise rates on November 5. The October 19 OIS snapshot assigns a 93.2% probability to a 25bps hike, implying Bank Rate rising from 3.75% to approximately 3.98%. A Reuters survey published October 15 showed similarly strong expectations among economists, with 54 of 63 forecasting an increase to 4.00%.
However, agreement weakens considerably beyond November. OIS pricing assigns a 51.6% probability to another hike at the December 17 meeting, followed by 75.6% at the February 2027 meeting. These are individual meeting probabilities, rather than cumulative odds. The implied policy rate reaches 4.30% in February and 4.79% by September 2027, equivalent to approximately four cumulative quarter-point increases from the current rate.
- November 5: 93.2% probability of a 25bps hike (3.75% → ~3.98%)
- December 17: 51.6% probability of another hike
- February 2027: 75.6% probability of another hike
- Implied path: ~4.30% by February 2027, ~4.79% by September 2027
Economists are substantially less convinced about the longer tightening cycle. Only 30 of 61 respondents in the Reuters survey expected another increase in the first quarter of 2027. The divergence suggests that markets are pricing a more extended period of monetary tightening than the economist consensus supports. Moreover, the latest implied rate path is marginally below that of a week earlier, indicating that expectations for further hikes have not been strengthening uniformly.
The distinction matters for Sterling. A November hike that is already almost fully priced may provide limited fresh support on its own. The more significant repricing opportunity lies in whether incoming evidence brings December tightening closer to certainty or raises doubts about the broader rate path.
Bailey’s Caution Contrasts With Hawkish MPC Members
The Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% in September by a 6–3 vote, with Huw Pill, Megan Greene and Catherine Mann favoring an increase to 4.00%. The split revealed substantial support for further tightening even before the latest inflation developments. However, the majority, including Bailey, preferred to wait for additional evidence.
Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, Bailey described evidence of second-round inflation effects as “quite subdued” so far, while emphasizing that it was too early to reach firm conclusions. Businesses were struggling to pass higher energy costs on to customers and were responding partly through cost reductions and pressure on margins. Bailey also acknowledged that the economy had proved more resilient than previously expected.
His assessment contrasts with warnings from more hawkish MPC members that waiting for clear evidence of persistent inflation could leave policy tightening too late. In particular, wage settlements in early 2027 could reveal second-round pressures only after they have become more firmly established.
The disagreement is therefore not simply about whether inflation is too high, but how quickly the BoE should respond to risks that are not yet fully visible. Bailey’s remarks provide support for a measured pace, while the existing dissenters and persistent inflation concerns underpin expectations for further tightening.
UK Wages and Services CPI Become the Critical Tests
This week’s economic calendar offers several opportunities to test the argument for an extended tightening cycle. Tuesday’s labor-market report will be important for assessing whether domestic wage pressures are becoming more persistent or continuing to ease. The latest available figures showed unemployment at 4.9% and regular pay growth at 3.5%, with private-sector regular pay growth having slowed substantially from a year earlier.
Private-sector wages and payroll employment deserve particular attention. Stronger pay growth would reinforce concerns that businesses face persistent labor costs, potentially increasing the risk of broader price pressures. Conversely, softer wage growth and continued employment weakness would strengthen the case for allowing existing monetary restraint more time to work through the economy.
Wednesday’s September CPI report is likely to carry even greater weight. Headline inflation stood at 3.1% in August, with core inflation at 2.6% and services inflation at 3.4%. Forecasts point to headline inflation rising toward approximately 3.4–3.5%, largely reflecting higher energy costs. Such an increase would not, by itself, establish that underlying inflation pressures are becoming more persistent.
The more important test is whether services and core inflation accelerate beyond the previous readings, particularly if accompanied by resilient private-sector pay. That combination would strengthen the argument for another increase soon after November. If headline inflation rises mainly because of energy while underlying measures remain contained, Bailey’s more cautious position would gain support.
Friday’s retail sales and flash PMI releases will provide additional information on domestic demand and business pricing conditions. Their significance will depend particularly on whether activity and price components point to persistent inflation or weakening demand. Thursday’s scheduled remarks from Bailey may also offer further clarification, although the speaking timetable requires confirmation.
- Unemployment: 4.9%; regular pay growth: 3.5%
- Headline CPI (August): 3.1%
- Core CPI: 2.6%
- Services CPI: 3.4%
- September CPI forecast: ~3.4–3.5%
Economic Resilience Meets Growth and Fiscal Constraints
Recent UK activity data have provided some support for the BoE’s tightening outlook. August GDP increased 0.1% mom, compared with expectations for a 0.1% contraction, while growth over the three months to August strengthened to 0.7%. Manufacturing output increased 1.2%, suggesting that the economy has been more resilient than anticipated.
However, the recovery remains uneven. Services output was flat in August, construction continued to weaken, and payroll employment has shown signs of deterioration. The combination of modest growth and softer labor demand complicates the case for a prolonged tightening cycle, particularly if inflation pressures remain concentrated in energy rather than spreading into wages and services.
Fiscal developments add another layer of uncertainty. Chancellor Rachel Healey is scheduled to deliver the Autumn Budget on October 28, accompanied by updated Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts. Elevated gilt yields and concerns about limited fiscal headroom could constrain government policy choices and influence broader financial conditions.
For Sterling, this means further BoE tightening is not automatically positive. Higher interest rates may support the currency through yield differentials, but an extended cycle could also weigh more heavily on growth and financial conditions. The balance between inflation persistence and economic resilience will determine how much support additional tightening expectations can provide.
ActionForex’s Technical View: GBP/USD 1.3341 Holds the Reversal Key

The recovery has been accompanied by improving momentum on the four-hour chart, where MACD has strengthened alongside a rising momentum trendline. articles.title: BOJ chief says underlying inflation 'quite close' to price goal - Yahoo Finance

articles.full_text:
By Leika Kihara
TOKYO, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said underlying inflation is "quite close" to the central bank's 2% target with strong global AI demand adding to inflationary pressure from a tight job market, signalling scope for further rate increases.
The remarks came ahead of the central bank's key policy meeting later this month, where it will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts which will be scrutinised by markets for clues on the next interest rate-hike timing.
"It is becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around our 2% target," Ueda told parliament on Monday.
While rising raw material costs from the Middle East conflict were pushing up inflation, a tight job market and moderate economic recovery were also applying demand-driven price pressure, Ueda said.
"Very strong global AI demand is boosting capital expenditure and exports, thereby pushing up prices for a wide range of goods," he said.
Ueda also said raising interest rates at an appropriate pace would help avoid spikes in bond yields.
"As underlying inflation approaches 2% and financial conditions remain accommodative, failing to adjust our policy rate appropriately could push up long-term interest rates by stoking market concern over an inflation overshoot," he said.
The BOJ has a two-day policy meeting that concludes on October 30. Having just raised rates in September, many in the BOJ are cautious about delivering another hike this month and prefer to gauge more data on how past rate increases have affected financial conditions, sources have told Reuters.
Many market players expect the BOJ to keep interest rates steady at 1.25% but drop hints that leave open scope for a hike to 1.5% as early as December.
CONTROLLING DEBT ISSUANCE
Japanese government bond (JGB) yields have risen on prospects of further BOJ rate hikes and concerns that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's big spending plans could worsen the country's already strained finances.
When asked by an opposition lawmaker about the impact of fiscal spending on inflation, Ueda said increased expenditure would push up price and wage growth by stimulating the economy.
But if increased fiscal spending boosts Japan's supply capacity, that in turn could help moderate inflation in the long run, he added.
Ueda reiterated that emergency bond-buying would be reserved for episodes of sharp yield rises or serious market dysfunction.
Speaking in the same parliament session, Takaichi dismissed suggestions by some analysts that her administration's policies had triggered the selloff in the yen and JGBs.

Bank of Japan (BoJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Monday that underlying inflation near the 2% target. Ueda further stated that if bank raises short-term policy rate, long-term interest rates likely to rise steadily with policy.
 Underlying inflation near 2% target. 
Anchoring core inflation near 2% grows more crucial. 
Japan experiencing positive loop of increasing wages, recovering prices. 
Middle East conflict is driving up energy and other supply-driven inflation pressures. 
Robust global al demand driving up domestic capex, exports and various goods prices as demand-led inflation. 
Japan's steady economic recovery and tight labor market also fuel inflation. 
No shift in central bank's fundamental bond taper approach. 
It is inappropriate to preannounce timing of emergency bond market measures. 
Bank will review market conditions including speed of long-term rate rise and signs of market instability to decide on intervention. 
If bank raises short-term policy rate, long-term interest rates likely to rise steadily with policy. 
Financial conditions stay accommodative. 
If policy rate isn't adjusted properly, market concerns about inflation risk could raise long-term rates. 
By implementing monetary policy properly to reach 2% inflation target, BoJ can help stabilize JGB market. 
At the time of writing, the USD/JPY pair is down 0.13% on the day at 157.80.
Ueda’s 7/10 FXS Speechtracker score is slightly below the 7.4/10 historic average, but the emphasis on “underlying inflation near 2%” and a “positive loop” of wages and prices marks a mildly hawkish tilt versus Japan’s past disinflation narrative. The focus on anchoring core inflation at 2%, robust global demand lifting exports and capex, and a tight labor market fueling inflation all support a gradual shift away from ultra-emergency settings, which is modestly supportive for the Yen.
At the same time, Ueda stresses no change in the fundamental bond taper approach and refuses to preannounce emergency bond measures, signaling caution and a desire to avoid destabilizing the JGB market. The message that properly calibrated rate hikes would allow long-term yields to rise “steadily” while keeping financial conditions accommodative suggests a controlled normalization path, limiting upside for the Yen in the near term but reinforcing a slow, hawkish-leaning bias over the medium term.
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) is the Japanese central bank, which sets monetary policy in the country. Its mandate is to issue banknotes and carry out currency and monetary control to ensure price stability, which means an inflation target of around 2%.
The Bank of Japan embarked in an ultra-loose monetary policy in 2013 in order to stimulate the economy and fuel inflation amid a low-inflationary environment. The bank’s policy is based on Quantitative and Qualitative Easing (QQE), or printing notes to buy assets such as government or corporate bonds to provide liquidity. In 2016, the bank doubled down on its strategy and further loosened policy by first introducing negative interest rates and then directly controlling the yield of its 10-year government bonds. In March 2024, the BoJ lifted interest rates, effectively retreating from the ultra-loose monetary policy stance.
The Bank’s massive stimulus caused the Yen to depreciate against its main currency peers. This process exacerbated in 2022 and 2023 due to an increasing policy divergence between the Bank of Japan and other main central banks, which opted to increase interest rates sharply to fight decades-high levels of inflation. The BoJ’s policy led to a widening differential with other currencies, dragging down the value of the Yen. This trend partly reversed in 2024, when the BoJ decided to abandon its ultra-loose policy stance.
A weaker Yen and the spike in global energy prices led to an increase in Japanese inflation, which exceeded the BoJ’s 2% target. The prospect of rising salaries in the country – a key element fuelling inflation – also contributed to the move.

articles.full_text:
“I have always been diligent with my repayments, so my credit score had improved organically over time. It helped in lowering my interest rate,” he says.
Like Tiwari, several borrowers with strong credit profiles, including an impeccable repayment track record, are finding that their diligent behaviour can earn them better deals from lenders. This matters more as borrowing costs are set to rise. On 7 October, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifted its monetary policy stance from neutral to calibrated tightening, signalling that further rate hikes remain a possibility. Economists expect the central bank to hike the repo rate by 75 basis points (one basis point equals 0.01 percentage point) by April 2027.
For home loan borrowers, it’s more important than ever to keep their credit profiles in good shape and explore opportunities to negotiate a lower rate with their lenders. Even a modest interest-rate reduction can translate into substantial savings.
Credit score to the rescue
All retail floating-rate loans sanctioned by banks after 1 October 2019 are linked to an external benchmark, typically the repo rate. Banks must pass on repo rate changes to borrowers, ensuring better transparency and transmission than older base rate- or marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) loans. However, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) are exempt from this regime.
The effective home loan rate essentially comprises the external benchmark chosen by banks (repo in the majority of cases), operating costs and credit risk premium. While the RBI sets the repo rate, the spread is the additional amount a lender charges over the benchmark rate. The RBI’s Commercial Banks – Interest Rates on Advances Directions, 2025 leave the spread to banks. However, banks must follow a board-approved policy for setting spreads. “The other spread components may be reduced by banks for a loan category earlier than three years for customer retention, on justifiable grounds, in a non-discriminatory manner, and in terms of the bank’s policy,” the circular says.
ALSO READ | Home loan closed? 5 smart ways to use your surplus EMI money for insurance, retirement and emergencies
The policy must specify the components of the spread and the range applicable to each borrower category. Therefore, the spread can vary across lenders and borrower categories. “The credit risk premium charged to an existing borrower shall not be increased except on account of deterioration in the credit risk profile of the customer or change in tenor premium,” RBI directions state.
Some banks transparently disclose differential effective interest rates for various borrower categories, depending on their credit scores, on their websites. For instance, Bank of India currently offers 7.35% annually to those with scores above 840, 7.5% for scores of 825-839, and 7.65% for scores of 760-799. Non-salaried borrowers in the last category pay 0.1 percentage point more. Rate grids vary across banks, but credit profiles remain a key factor even when not explicitly disclosed.
Ordinarily, banks can review operating costs once every three years. The credit risk premium, however, can be revised only when the borrower’s credit profile changes. This gives borrowers whose credit scores have improved an opportunity to negotiate a lower interest rate with their lenders.
Take the case of Ahaan Pandit, a finance professional based in Bengaluru. He took a Rs.46 lakh home loan at 8% in 2018, when his credit score stood at 730. Over the years, his score improved to 810, but the bank did not lower the credit risk premium on his loan. In 2024, he realised the lender offered lower rates to borrowers with credit scores above 800. “I emailed my bank, highlighted the improvement in my credit score and asked it to reprice my loan,” he says. The result? The bank agreed, resulting in interest savings of nearly Rs.14 lakh.
ALSO READ | RBI repo rate hike: How home loan borrowers can reduce EMI and interest burden
While Pandit and Tiwari belong to a growing tribe of financially savvy borrowers who know how to negotiate better deals, awareness of the opportunity remains low. “Close to 70% of the borrowers on our platform are overpaying due to wider spreads on underlying loans,” says Kunal Shah, Co-founder of SURE Financial, a loan analytics start-up.
However, a higher credit score does not automatically translate into a lower interest rate. “The sanctioned spread reflects the borrower’s profile at the time of sanction.
The bank has no obligation to re-underwrite the loan just because the score has improved. However, borrowers can cite their improved credit scores to seek a reduction in the spread,” says Vipul Patel, Founder of MortgageWorld, a loan consultancy firm.
You must take the initiative to request a rate revision. “The lender will not change the risk premium or spread automatically. It depends on a request from the borrower,” Patel adds.
The bank will use its discretion on repricing. A higher score alone will not ensure the entire credit risk premium comes down. “You should seek a full reassessment covering income, leverage, repayment history, collateral and loan-to-value (LTV). Where the credit assessment has substantially changed, the borrower can ask for a premium review under the loan agreement,” he adds.
How a higher credit score can lower home loan costs
Assumptions: 1. Ten EMIs have been paid from December 2025 to September 2026 at 8% per annum; 2. The rate change (due to the RBI repo rate hike) takes effect from November 2026 (month 11). 3. Post repo hike, borrower increases EMI, not tenure. 4. Borrower retains this increased EMI post negotiations with lender. Source: MortgageWorld.in
Making the switch
Before approaching your lender to renegotiate your home loan rate, understand the terms and conditions of your loan agreement. Establish the external benchmark your loan is linked to, the current benchmark rate, the contractual spread and the effective interest rate. “Ask for the spread breakup. Check the loan agreement for the credit-risk review clause and the reset frequency, which must be at least quarterly,” says Patel.
While banks must review rates at least once every quarter for external benchmark-linked loans, check your loan agreement to understand the terms governing a review of the credit risk premium. These will vary across lenders. Some may conduct a half-yearly assessment and link revisions to improvements in your credit score, while others may consider several factors when reassessing your credit profile.
“Gather the latest credit bureau report, your repayment track record, updated income documents and evidence of lower leverage or improved LTV,” advises Patel. Also, compare existing lender’s rates and policies with those of competitors when you make your case. “You can start the process by requesting banks to reduce credit risk premium if your score has improved. An email or conversation with your relationship manager will do the needful,” says Shah of SURE. Banks may levy a one-time fee to switch to a lower rate, ranging from Rs.3,500-6,000 depending on their internal policies. RBI rules require banks to allow borrowers with older MCLR- or Base Rate linked loans to switch to external benchmark-linked rate (EBLR) loans without charges, except for reasonable administrative and legal costs.
How to boost credit scores
Improving your credit score requires consistent credit discipline over time, not quick fixes. Credit discipline— timely repayment of home loan EMIs and credit card bills as well as clearing overdue amounts—can strengthen your credit profile. “It is important to understand that the credit score reflects a long-term view of the borrower and it takes some time for such actions to reflect in the score,” says Manish Jain, Country Managing Director, Experian India.
You should also check your credit reports regularly to identify discrepancies. “Errors in the report, outdated information or fraudulent activity could affect the score, even when repayments are made on time,” says Jain. Credit information companies –TransUnion CIBIL, Experian, Equifax and CRIF High Mark–are mandated to allow borrowers access to their credit report at least once a year, free of charge. You can also access your score and report through your banks.
Avoid taking on multiple unsecured credit products, such as personal loans and credit cards, without assessing your repayment capacity. Applying for several credit cards within a short period is also not wise, as this can signal excessive dependence on credit.
“Also, assess the repayment habits of the primary borrower before becoming a co-applicant on a loan. Missed payments by the primary borrower can affect your credit score,” says Jain.

Nalgonda-based Ruthvick Reddy learnt this the hard way when he agreed to be the guarantor for an acquaintance’s loan. “My credit score was affected earlier, falling to around 740, as the borrower had delayed repayments,” he says. Consequently, when he applied for a home loan in 2019, he was charged an interest rate of 9.05%. Since then, his score has improved to 770. “I worked towards building a strong credit profile by making regular credit card payments. My improved credit score helped me reduce my interest outgo after I negotiated with my bank in 2024,” says Reddy.

Gold prices edged lower on October 19th, pressured by a stronger US dollar and rising US Treasury yields.
 Meanwhile, investors are awaiting the Federal Reserve's policy decision next week, with forecasts suggesting the central bank will keep interest rates unchanged.
 At 6:09 PM GMT on October 19th (1:09 AM on October 20th in Vietnam time), spot gold prices fell 0.4% to $4,147.87 per ounce. Gold futures for December 2026 delivery in the US closed down 0.5% at $4,160.10 per ounce.
 The US dollar edged higher, making gold, which is priced in the dollar, more expensive for holders of other currencies. Meanwhile, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose 0.6%.
 Fawad Razaqzada, a market analyst at Forex.com, a foreign exchange and contract for difference brokerage, said the market is concerned that central banks will have to continue tightening monetary policy to control inflation, thereby pushing yields higher. With yields remaining high, gold investors are considering whether investing in bonds might be a better option at this time.
 In September 2026, the Fed raised interest rates by another 0.25 percentage points, marking the first increase this year.
 Mr. Razaqzada believes the issue is not just whether the Fed will raise interest rates next week or wait until December, but also about the central bank's policy message. According to him, if the Fed sends a more hawkish signal on monetary policy, gold prices could continue to weaken in the short term.
 According to CME's FedWatch tool, traders assess the likelihood of the Fed keeping interest rates unchanged this month at 82.8%, while the probability of a rate hike in December remains at 90%. 
 Gold is often seen as an asset that helps hedge against inflation. However, when interest rates rise, the appeal of gold diminishes because the precious metal does not yield returns like bonds or other income-generating assets. This is the measure of inflation that the Fed prefers to use in its monetary policy planning.

articles.title: [Insight] AI Investment Boom Adds Pressure to Bond Markets as Central Banks Warn of Financial Risks - Korea IT Times
articles.summary: [Insight] AI Investment Boom Adds Pressure to Bond Markets as Central Banks Warn of Financial Risks  Korea IT Times
articles.full_text:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) headquarters in Washington, D.C. The IMF has identified a potential repricing of AI-related assets and rising sovereign bond yields as significant risks to global financial stability. / Photo: APK, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
Massive investment in artificial intelligence is emerging as a new factor shaping global bond markets. Corporate demand for capital is rising as investment expands beyond semiconductors and data centers into power grids and telecommunications infrastructure. Although AI is widely regarded as a driver of global economic growth, the enormous capital required before productivity gains and investment returns fully materialize is adding pressure to financial markets.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) recently identified a potential repricing of AI-related assets and a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields as major risks to financial stability. The European Central Bank (ECB) has also expressed concern about tighter financial conditions resulting from higher long-term interest rates and concentrated exposures to AI-related financial assets. These developments suggest that assessing the AI industry's prospects increasingly requires examining financing structures and debt-servicing capacity alongside growth potential.
AI Investment Becomes a New Factor in Global Financing Costs
At the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, the implications of rising AI investment for interest rates, inflation and financial stability attracted growing attention. According to Reuters, recent increases in global bond yields have reflected several factors, including large fiscal deficits, inflation concerns and rising demand for capital associated with AI infrastructure investment. While AI may improve productivity over the longer term, the immediate effects include greater demand for capital and energy to build data centers and power infrastructure.
Corporate AI investment decisions are becoming increasingly connected to bond markets. When major cloud providers issue bonds or raise external financing to build data centers and acquire semiconductors, their funding requirements compete with borrowing demand from other companies and governments. In an environment where investors demand higher yields, financing costs can also increase for businesses and households. However, recent increases in sovereign bond yields cannot be attributed to AI investment alone, as fiscal deficits, energy prices and inflation expectations are also important drivers.
IMF Warns of AI Investment Repricing and Sovereign Bond Risks
In its October Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF identified three potential triggers of financial instability: a repricing of AI-related assets, a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields and cyberattacks. The Fund warned that valuations could come under pressure if AI investment and profitability prove weaker or less sustainable than expected. It also highlighted the potential for rising leverage, concentrated exposures and circular financing arrangements among companies to amplify market shocks.
The IMF's concerns extend beyond the growth prospects of AI companies to the financial structures supporting their expansion. When major technology companies invest in AI developers that subsequently purchase cloud computing and semiconductor services from those same investors, capital flows and revenue streams become interconnected. Such arrangements can accelerate infrastructure development, but they may also expose investors and suppliers to simultaneous losses if end-user demand and profitability fall short of expectations.
AI infrastructure financing is also becoming increasingly important in corporate bond markets. According to the IMF report, major hyperscale cloud providers have raised more than $100 billion through bond financing since early 2025 and may require additional external funding as investment expands. Nevertheless, the IMF assessed the immediate financial stability risks associated with this borrowing as limited, citing the generally strong balance sheets and cash-generating capacity of these companies. Its assessment points to the need for continued scrutiny of investment commitments and financing structures rather than suggesting that a systemic crisis has already emerged.
The IMF also warned that an adjustment in AI-related investments could produce more severe consequences if accompanied by rising sovereign bond yields and existing financial vulnerabilities. A broad sell-off in risky assets and tighter lending conditions could transmit financing pressures from technology companies to investment and employment across the wider economy. However, major banks were assessed as generally resilient under stress scenarios combining AI, bond market and energy shocks. Preventing vulnerabilities at weaker banks and nonbank financial institutions from spreading through the financial system remains an important priority.
ECB Warns of Slower Growth and Concentrated AI Exposures
ECB President Christine Lagarde said at the International Monetary and Financial Committee meeting on October 17 that long-term interest rates had risen markedly since the ECB's previous monetary policy meeting, tightening financial conditions. She explained that this development could weigh on economic growth and reduce the extent to which higher energy prices are passed through to consumer inflation compared with earlier projections. Her remarks reflected the effects of higher borrowing costs on both economic activity and price developments.
Lagarde also acknowledged that AI investment was supporting economic activity and international trade. She indicated that investment in AI and digital technologies could contribute to Europe's medium-term growth prospects. From a financial stability perspective, however, she warned that uncertainty surrounding AI adoption and concentrated exposures to AI-related assets could amplify market shocks. Concentrated positions among nonbank financial institutions and their connections with banks could become channels through which financial stress spreads.
The ECB's assessment does not mean that AI investment is directly responsible for rising interest rates. Rather, it distinguishes the growth benefits of AI investment from the separate risks associated with higher long-term yields and concentrated financial exposures. Data center projects are particularly sensitive to financing costs because they require substantial upfront capital and often take years to generate returns. Even if AI companies maintain strong growth prospects, higher borrowing costs can alter project economics and investment schedules.
China's Central Bank Calls for Closer Monitoring of Advanced-Economy Fiscal Risks
People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng also urged the IMF on October 17 to strengthen surveillance of fiscal risks in major advanced economies and their international spillover effects. According to Reuters, Pan emphasized the need to give greater weight to financial factors, including cross-border capital flows, when analyzing global imbalances. His remarks reflected concerns that large fiscal deficits and rising borrowing costs in major economies could affect financial markets elsewhere.
Pan did not identify AI investment itself as a direct cause of a financial crisis. His remarks focused instead on the need to manage the global consequences of advanced-economy fiscal policies and international capital movements. Nevertheless, as large-scale AI infrastructure investment adds to global demand for financing, fiscal sustainability and international financial stability are becoming increasingly important policy considerations.
South Korea's AI Export Boom Faces a New Test in Global Capital Markets
For South Korea, the financial sustainability of global AI investment is becoming a critical variable in the semiconductor industry's outlook. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix stand to benefit from sustained demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and server memory. Yet much of that demand ultimately depends on capital expenditure by overseas cloud providers and AI infrastructure operators. Their financing decisions can therefore influence Korea's export performance even when domestic chipmakers remain technologically competitive.
This creates an important distinction between semiconductor orders and sustainable end-market demand. A cloud provider may continue purchasing advanced memory while expanding data centers through debt financing, but the durability of that spending depends on utilization rates, AI service revenue and cash generation. If financing costs rise or expected returns weaken, customers may delay new facilities or revise procurement schedules. For Korean suppliers, the resulting risk is not necessarily an immediate collapse in orders but a potential slowdown in future demand growth.
The exposure extends beyond memory manufacturers. Korean semiconductor equipment suppliers, power infrastructure companies and other businesses linked to data center expansion may also be affected by changes in global investment schedules. Delays in grid connections, cooling systems or construction approvals can postpone semiconductor deployment even when chips are available. Announced capital expenditure and completed infrastructure therefore need to be evaluated separately.
The policy implications are equally significant. South Korea's industrial strategy cannot rely solely on expanding semiconductor production capacity in anticipation of continued global AI spending. Policymakers and companies need to examine the financial resilience of major customers, the pace of actual infrastructure deployment and the relationship between AI investment and recurring commercial revenue. These indicators can provide a more reliable assessment of demand than headline investment commitments alone.

articles.title: "What if the market crashes again?" Even as new margin trading (leveraged investing) is blocked... The fear of "forced liquidation" ticks away - 머니투데이
articles.summary: "What if the market crashes again?" Even as new margin trading (leveraged investing) is blocked... The fear of "forced liquidation" ticks away  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
Will the risks remain even if margin trading is blocked?... The fear of "short selling" lurking in a plunging market
As financial regulators move to curb "margin investing (investing with debt)"—or borrowing to invest—the risk of forced liquidations on existing credit loans has emerged as a new source of market instability amid heightened volatility, including recent sharp declines in the stock market. Although measures taking effect on the 19th aim to prevent excessive concentration of credit loans in specific stocks, this does not eliminate the risks already accumulated from margin investing (investing with debt).
Market participants are concerned that further declines in stock prices could trigger forced liquidations on existing loans, thereby exacerbating the downturn in the stock market. It is pointed out that, separate from efforts by financial regulators and securities firms to curb new borrowing, there is a growing need to manage the risks associated with existing margin financing.
◇New Margin Investing (Investing with Debt) Is Blocked, but Existing Risks Remain... The Dilemma of Regulation
According to the financial investment industry on the 18th, the Financial Services Commission held an emergency review meeting on the 15th in response to the sharp stock market decline and urged financial companies, including securities firms, to refrain from indiscriminate credit extension. Financial Services Commissioner Lee Eui-woon emphasized the risks of investing that relies excessively on debt and credit, and requested that all possible measures be taken for customer protection and risk management.
This directive from financial regulators aligns with the concentrated management measures for margin trading that take effect on the 19th. The Korea Financial Investment Association and 10 comprehensive securities firms formulated a plan last month to strengthen voluntary management of margin trading. The core of the plan is to impose stricter controls on new margin loans for specific stocks if margin lending for those stocks exceeds 15% of the firm's total margin lending portfolio.
Each investment firm can lower the loan limit per investor for a given stock or raise the margin requirement, which is the percentage of the purchase price that investors must cover with their own funds. The specific management methods are determined at the discretion of each securities firm.
A notable aspect is that the new measures apply only to new investments, not existing margin loans. The Korea Financial Investment Association explained that this was done to minimize market impact. Investors who previously borrowed money to buy stocks are not required to immediately repay their loans solely because of the implementation of the new standards. Existing loans will continue to be managed under the previous management system, including terms such as maturity dates and collateral maintenance ratios stipulated in the original agreements.
There is also a dilemma related to market stability in margin financing regulations. Just because margin investing (investing with debt) is considered risky, pressuring investors to reduce their existing loans all at once could force them to sell their held stocks to repay the debt. While the market may be able to absorb such selling volume during periods of stable stock prices, it is highly likely to act as additional selling pressure in situations where stock prices are plummeting.
◇Existing margin investing (leveraged investing) still carries the risk of forced liquidation... concerns over chain selling remain
Even if new regulations do not apply to existing loans, the risk of forced liquidation remains. Credit financing is a transaction in which investors use borrowed funds to purchase stocks and other securities, providing them as collateral. If stock prices fall and the value of the collateral drops below a certain level, securities firms demand that investors replenish the shortfall. If an investor fails to deposit cash or additional collateral by the specified deadline, the securities firm initiates forced liquidation, selling the collateralized shares to recover the loan amount.
In particular, during a sharp market decline, the collateral values of multiple investors may fall simultaneously. If more investors fail to provide additional collateral, there is an increased likelihood that forced liquidation volumes will be dumped onto the market all at once. This can trigger a vicious cycle in which forced sales drive stock prices further down, leading to insufficient collateral among other investors and subsequent forced liquidations.
Credit margin forced liquidations surged even during this year's stock market crash. According to the office of People Power Party lawmaker Kim Sang-hoon, the total value of credit margin forced liquidation transactions at 10 major securities firms in March, when the market was significantly shaken by Middle East-related shocks, reached approximately 180 billion won, nearly tripling from the previous month (61.2 billion won). In June as well, the amount of forced liquidations increased by 188% to 393.5 billion won compared to the previous month (136.8 billion won).
There have been cases in which large-scale forced liquidations of margin trading occurred even during past market crashes. According to data from the Financial Supervisory Service, the total value of forced liquidations of margin loans at 10 major securities firms in August 2024 was 260.2 billion won, recording the highest monthly amount for that year. On August 5 of that month, the KOSPI index plunged by 8.8%, and the KOSDAQ index fell by 11.3%.
The risk of forced liquidation that can materialize in a sharp market decline is difficult to resolve solely through the stock-specific credit loan concentration management measures taking effect on the 19th. As these measures restrict new credit loans supplied to specific stocks to prevent further concentration of risk, the collateral shortfalls and forced liquidation risks associated with previously accumulated credit loans must be managed separately.
It is also difficult to suppress forced liquidations themselves. This is because if loans are not recovered even when the collateral value declines, the credit risk of securities firms may increase. On the other hand, analysts point out that there are challenges in risk management, as concentrated forced liquidations by multiple securities firms on specific stocks or at particular times can amplify downward pressure on the market.
Accordingly, as stock market volatility expands, it is pointed out that one must carefully examine not only the increasing trend in new margin loans but also the risk of insufficient collateral on existing loans and the possibility of forced liquidation.
A financial investment industry official stated, "It is necessary to assess how much additional margin calls have increased due to the sharp drop in stock prices and whether forced liquidations are likely to be concentrated at specific times or in particular stocks." The official added, "Investors should also recognize that the new regulations do not protect existing loans and need to verify the maintenance margin ratio applicable to them, the deadline for additional margin deposits, and the conditions for forced liquidation."
The shield that had been absorbing foreign investors’ selling pressure has vanished... KOSPI pushed down to 5,400; what is needed for a rebound
The domestic stock market is being shaken by supply-demand imbalances. As foreign investors dump their holdings, no clear buyer has emerged to absorb the selling pressure. Retail investors, who had previously absorbed foreign sell-offs, have seen their buying capacity weaken due to the burden of margin trading and a decline in investor sentiment. Moreover, the “breakwater” provided by share buybacks from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix has also disappeared. The KOSPI index fell to the 5,400 level for the first time since July, while the KOSPI 200 Volatility Index (V-KOSPI) crossed the 50th-point threshold—marking the “fear zone”—for the first time since late August on the 15th.
According to the Korea Financial Investment Association on the 17th, investor deposits stood at 96.9121 trillion won as of the 15th. Deposits had fallen below the 100th trillion won mark for the first time since the 21st of last month, dropping from 97.4280 trillion won on the 14th. Investor deposits refer to cash remaining in securities accounts and are considered "ammunition" for stock investment. In contrast, the balance of credit trading financing was recorded at 32.7499 trillion won. This figure had decreased to the 27th trillion won range on August 4 before surpassing 34 trillion won on the 13th of this month, indicating an upward trend. Consequently, funds awaiting investment in the stock market have decreased, while the burden of leveraged investment has increased.
Expanding margin trading can act as a kind of "time bomb," as it may trigger forced liquidations when stock prices plummet. If share prices fall and the collateral value drops, securities firms demand additional collateral from investors. If investors fail to meet this requirement within the specified deadline, the firms can forcibly sell their held shares. This process can create a vicious cycle in which a flood of selling pressure hits the market, driving stock prices even lower.
Forced liquidation activity was prominent over the three trading days following the activation of a sell-side sidecar (futures market circuit breaker) in the KOSPI market on the 13th. Margin call balances refer to amounts that investors failed to pay by the settlement date after purchasing stocks. articles.title: USD/JPY Holds Near 158 as Intervention Risk Caps Gains and Fed Hike Bets Ease - Markets.com
articles.summary: USD/JPY Holds Near 158 as Intervention Risk Caps Gains and Fed Hike Bets Ease  Markets.com
articles.full_text:
USD/JPY ended the week of October 12–16 near 158.00, as persistent US inflation supported the dollar while easing Treasury yields and concern about Japanese intervention limited its advance.
The pair reached approximately 158.95 during the week but failed to sustain a move through 159.00. On the downside, buying interest emerged around 157.50, leaving the exchange rate within a relatively narrow range despite significant changes in US interest-rate expectations.
The consolidation reflects competing policy pressures. Further Fed tightening could preserve support for the dollar, while the prospect of additional Bank of Japan rate increases gives investors a reason to reconsider yen selling.
The 159–160 area remains an important focus for intervention concerns. However, it should not be treated as an official trigger. The speed and disorderliness of a currency move, alongside statements from Japanese authorities, can matter as much as the exchange rate itself.
September’s US inflation figures initially strengthened the case for another interest-rate increase. Headline consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, accelerating from 3.4% in August. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased to 2.6%.
Consumer prices also rose 0.6% month on month, while the core measure increased 0.3%. The figures reinforced concern that inflation pressures remain persistent and that returning price growth to the Fed’s target could require restrictive monetary policy for longer.
For USD/JPY, the main transmission channel is the relative return available on dollar and yen assets. When investors anticipate higher US rates, Treasury yields can rise and make dollar-denominated investments more attractive.
However, inflation data do not determine the exchange rate in isolation. The market must also assess whether policymakers will respond immediately, how much tightening is already reflected in prices, and whether economic conditions could weaken.
Last week’s reversal in rate expectations demonstrated that distinction. Strong inflation increased concern about further tightening, but it did not establish a clear timetable for the Fed’s next move.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh avoided committing to a specific rate decision during his appearance in Bangkok. His comments indicated that recent economic developments had broadly followed policymakers’ expectations, without providing a firm signal for the October 27–28 meeting.
That restrained message helped reduce expectations of an imminent increase. Published market estimates placed October hike probabilities in the low-to-mid teens after his remarks, compared with roughly half or more earlier in the week. Exact readings varied with the observation time.
The repricing weakened one source of near-term dollar support. Treasury yields eased, reducing the momentum that had previously pushed USD/JPY toward the upper end of its range.
Nevertheless, a lower probability of an October increase does not necessarily imply that the tightening cycle has ended. Investors may instead be shifting their expectations toward a later meeting.
This distinction matters for the pair. A delay could limit immediate dollar gains, while expectations of persistently restrictive US policy could still help explain why USD/JPY has held above its recent support area.
Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda also maintained attention on monetary tightening, highlighting the importance of keeping underlying inflation anchored around the central bank’s 2% target.
His remarks identified exchange-rate movements among the factors relevant to the policy outlook. A weaker yen can increase the domestic cost of imported fuel, food and other goods, potentially adding to inflation pressures.
For currency markets, the question is whether those pressures change the expected timing or pace of BOJ rate increases.
Stronger expectations of Japanese tightening could support the yen by narrowing the anticipated interest-rate gap with the United States. Conversely, uncertainty over the timing of the next increase could leave the yen vulnerable when US yields rise.
Monetary policy and currency intervention are separate tools. Japan’s Ministry of Finance decides on foreign-exchange intervention, while the BOJ conducts operations on its behalf. Ueda’s inflation comments therefore should not be interpreted as confirmation that intervention is imminent.
Attention now turns to economic releases during October 19–23, including Friday’s US flash manufacturing and services purchasing managers’ indices.
The surveys could help investors assess whether business activity remains resilient alongside elevated price pressures. Their details may prove as important as the headline readings, particularly measures of input costs, selling prices, employment and new orders.
Stronger activity accompanied by rising prices could revive expectations of additional Fed tightening and support Treasury yields. That combination could give USD/JPY another opportunity to test 159.00.
A softer growth picture, particularly if price pressures also moderate, could reinforce expectations that the Fed can wait. Further declines in US yields would then increase attention on the lower boundary of the recent trading range.
Japanese policy expectations remain equally relevant. Evidence that the BOJ is moving closer to another increase could strengthen yen demand even if the dollar remains supported against other currencies.
The recent range provides clear reference points, although neither boundary guarantees a reversal.
The weekly high near 158.95 and the nearby 159.00 level form the first area to watch on the upside. A sustained break would bring 160.00 into greater focus, alongside closer scrutiny of Japanese official commentary.
On the downside, the 157.50–157.55 area marks the recent floor. A decisive move below it would suggest that buyers are losing control of the consolidation.
USD/JPY therefore enters the new week with a firm US inflation backdrop but less conviction about an immediate Fed response. Whether the pair can escape its range will depend on how US yields and Japanese rate expectations adjust to the next round of evidence.

articles.title: The 10-Year Treasury Is Above 5% for the First Time in Almost 20 Years. History Says This Is How the S&P 500 Index Will Perform Over the Next 12 Months. - The Motley Fool
articles.summary: The 10-Year Treasury Is Above 5% for the First Time in Almost 20 Years. History Says This Is How the S&P 500 Index Will Perform Over the Next 12 Months.  The Motley Fool
articles.full_text:
On the morning of Thursday, Oct. 15, the 10-year Treasury yield sat at 5.06%. It has been making headlines ever since it crossed 5% about three weeks ago. This is viewed by experts as being the most important number in global finance. That's because it sets the risk-free rate of return that anchors pricing, mortgages, corporate borrowing costs, and valuations across the entire economy.
Besides passing this threshold in late September, the 10-year Treasury yield last closed above 5% on July 19, 2007. Almost 20 years have passed since investors have seen it at this level. When rare events like this occur, it might be time to pay attention to what's going on.
Markets are extremely complex and interconnected, and the current situation might affect your portfolio. Investors naturally want to know what comes next for the stock market, and history says this is how the S&P 500 index could perform in the coming 12 months.
Drawing parallels to a different era
Over the 12 months following July 19, 2007, the popular stock market benchmark fell 19%. And over the subsequent five years, it was down 11%. This might draw a pessimistic outlook from investors.
In the four years leading up to it closing above 5% on that date in July 2007, the 10-year Treasury saw its yield rise 26%. This was supported by the Federal Reserve aggressively hiking the fed funds rate. The U.S. economy was registering strong growth, and one of the goals was to get ahead of above-average inflation.
That backdrop mimics what we see today. Just in the past 12 months, the 10-year Treasury yield has soared 26%. The central bank has started to raise rates due to stubborn inflation. And as was the case in July 2007, the S&P 500 is currently in all-time record territory and in the middle of a multiyear bull run.
After looking at the parallels, investors might have a gloomy view.
Why this time could be different
However, there are some important differences that shouldn't be ignored. After 2007, stocks performed poorly because of the onset of the Great Financial Crisis. Banks loaded up on risky subprime mortgages, packaging them into complex securities that were sold to third-party investors to raise capital to lend even more. This contributed to the real estate bubble popping, which rippled through the financial system.
What's more, in July 2007, the Treasury yield curve was inverted. The six-month bill was offering investors a higher yield than the 10-year note. This has historically been a dependable recession indicator. Right now, the yield curve is normal and positively sloped.
S&P 500 Index
Key Data Points
The banking sector today operates under stricter regulations, thanks in large part to the passing of the Dodd-Frank Act in July 2010. And the stock market is dominated by highly profitable and growing tech giants, led by leading artificial intelligence (AI) enterprises. It's not crazy to think that they could keep expanding in the years ahead, despite their huge size.
In the mid-2000s, businesses in the financial and energy sectors, for example, had much higher weightings in the S&P 500 than they do today. When it comes to leverage, growth, profits, and capital intensity, they aren't as attractive as technology companies.
Assume that time rewards patient investors
The S&P 500 index continues to march higher, but this doesn't prevent the investment community from living with constant fear, uncertainty, and doubt. Pessimism rules the day. Investors should remain optimistic about the long term, though. That's true even if history might suggest that the next 12 months to five years could be worse than anticipated.
It's never a bad idea to be bullish about the long term. That's not hard to do when you focus on owning high-quality companies for several years. Not paying too much attention to macroeconomic data points or using them as predictive tools also makes it incredibly easier.
Study history to sharpen your perspective. But stay the course. And invest early and often.

articles.title: RBI may need to raise repo rate to 6.25% as inflation risks persist: SBI Mutual Fund - https://www.indiagazette.com/
articles.summary: RBI may need to raise repo rate to 6.25% as inflation risks persist: SBI Mutual Fund  https://www.indiagazette.com/
articles.full_text:
ANI
                
18 Oct 2026, 17:35 GMT+10
            
New Delhi [India], October 18 (ANI): The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may need to raise its benchmark repo rate to at least 6.25 per cent to contain inflation risks, according to SBI Funds Management, an assessment that has gained relevance following the latest rise in retail and wholesale inflation.
In its October 2026 Market Outlook report, the fund house said further monetary tightening could be necessary even after the RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent earlier this month.
'From a real rate perspective, policy rates may need to move to at least 6.25% to enable a real rate around 1%,' the report stated.
The assessment implies another 75 basis points of rate increases from the current level, although the report does not specify a timeline.
The warning comes as India's retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September from 4.83 per cent in August, while wholesale inflation accelerated to 11.39 per cent from 9.92 per cent, according to government data released last week.
'Even with the current forward estimate on CPI inflation for FY27 at 5.20%, headline CPI remains almost 120bps above the 4% target. This clearly warrants additional policy actions going forward,' the report stated.
The RBI has projected inflation at 6 per cent in the third quarter of FY27 and 5.7 per cent in the fourth quarter, reflecting continued price pressures.
SBI Funds Management warned that elevated crude oil prices, potential food inflation and strong domestic demand could push inflation above the RBI's 6 per cent upper tolerance limit for two consecutive quarters.
'Accordingly, the near-term path for the policy rates is either a hike or hold with rate cuts being off the table,' it said.
The fund house also cautioned that surplus banking-system liquidity could weaken the effectiveness of rate hikes, making liquidity management important for controlling inflation.
The RBI's next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is scheduled for December 2-4, when it will review fresh inflation data before deciding on further interest rate action. (ANI)

articles.summary: Flexible Fed policy outlook boosts prospects for emerging market economies  https://greenpost.com.pk/
articles.full_text:
Islamabad Oct 17,2026: The US Federal Reserve’s flexible approach to future interest rate decisions offers emerging markets a potential reprieve from abrupt tightening in global financial conditions.
The Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4% in September after keeping rates unchanged for nine months. Its latest communication indicates that future decisions will depend on incoming economic data rather than a predetermined schedule of rate increases.
Recent US economic indicators have presented a mixed picture. Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September, while unemployment remained at 4.2%. Average hourly earnings rose 3% year-on-year, suggesting some moderation in labour market momentum and adding uncertainty to the outlook for further monetary tightening.
Inflation, however, remains above the Fed’s objective. US consumer prices increased 3.4% year-on-year in August,while inflation excluding food and energy stood at 2.4%. September inflation figures are scheduled for release on October 14 and are expected to influence market expectations ahead of the Fed’s October 27–28 meeting.
Ubaid Ullah Khan, former Unit Head at the State Bank of Pakistan, told Wealth Pakistan that the significance of the Fed’s policy flexibility for emerging economies lay less in whether interest rates eventually increased again and more in whether further tightening occurred gradually enough for global financial markets to adjust.
“When monetary policy is not tied to consecutive rate increases, emerging markets get some breathing space. It reduces the risk of sudden repricing in currencies, bonds and external financing and gives central banks more room to manage their own policy response,” he said.
Khan cautioned that greater flexibility in the timing of interest rate decisions should not be interpreted as a shift towards monetary easing, particularly while inflation remained a concern for US policymakers.
“The Fed is still signalling concern about inflation. For emerging economies, the benefit is that the adjustment may be spread over time rather than delivered through a rapid sequence of rate increases. That distinction matters significantly for countries managing external debt and foreign exchange pressures,” he added.
The Fed’s data-dependent approach has implications extending well beyond the United States because changes in American interest rates influence global borrowing costs, international investment decisions andthe movement of capital between developed and emerging economies.
When US monetary policy becomes more restrictive, higher returns on dollar-denominated assets can increase pressure on emerging-market currencies and make it more expensive for governments and businesses to raise financing in international markets.
Conversely, greater predictability in the pace of monetary tightening can reduce uncertainty and provide additional time for emerging economies to manage debt repayments, strengthen foreign exchange reserves and adjust domestic financial policies.
The importance of these developments has increased as emerging economies have become more exposed to international portfolio investment and shifts in global financial conditions.
According to research published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) this year, portfolio debt liabilities now average around 15% of GDP across emerging markets, compared with approximately 9% in 2006.
The research found that nonbank investors supply about 80% of this capital, highlighting the growing role of international investment funds and other nonbank financial institutions in emerging-market financing.
Separate IMF research identified changes in US monetary policy as an important driver of emerging-market borrowing spreads and capital flows, demonstrating how shifts in expectations about the Fed’s future decisions can influence financing conditions across developing economies.
Adil Mustafa, Director Compliance at Khushhali Bank, said greater predictability in US monetary policy could temporarily improve funding conditions for emerging economies by reducing uncertainty surrounding dollar liquidity and international borrowing costs.
“For banks and businesses in developing markets, the challenge is not only the level of US interest rates but the volatility surrounding their future direction. A more flexible and data-dependent approach allows institutions to plan liquidity, foreign currency exposure and refinancing requirements with greater confidence,” he told Wealth Pakistan.
Mustafa said the impact of the Fed’s policy direction could also extend to international investor behaviour, particularly in countries that depend on external financing and foreign portfolio inflows.
“When markets fear rapid US tightening, international investors tend to become more defensive and emerging market assets face greater pressure. If rate increases are spaced out, it can reduce that immediate pressure, although countries with weak external positions will still need to maintain strong buffers,” he said.
The changing outlook for US interest rates is particularly relevant for developing economies already facing substantial external debt obligations and elevated refinancing costs.
According to World Bank estimates, low- and middle-income countries paid a record $415 billion in interest on external debt in 2024, while their combined external debt reached $8.9 trillion.
These figures underscore the financial pressures facing developing economies, where high borrowing costs can constrain fiscal resources, limit development spending and increase the burden of servicing existing obligations.
For countries such as Pakistan, which must manage external financing requirements alongside domestic economic priorities, greater stability in global interest rate expectations planning could offer some relief for financial planning.
However, experts stressed that any improvement in international financing conditions would depend on broader economic fundamentals, including foreign exchange reserves, debt sustainability, investor confidence and the availability of external financing.
Mustafa said financial institutions and businesses in emerging economies needed to use periods of reduced market volatility to improve liquidity planning and manage foreign currency exposure more effectively.
He emphasised that a slower pace of US monetary tightening would not eliminate the risks associated with elevated global interest rates, particularly for economies with weak external positions.
Khan similarly cautioned that the current flexibility in US monetary policy should be viewed as an opportunity for emerging economies to strengthen their financial resilience rather than increase their dependence on external borrowing.
He said countries facing substantial refinancing requirements needed to focus on extending debt maturities, building up reserve buffers and reducing vulnerabilities to sudden changes in international capital flows.
“For emerging economies, breathing room is valuable only if it is used to lengthen maturities, strengthen reserves and reduce refinancing vulnerabilities. The global interest rate environment remains restrictive, so policy flexibility in Washington should be treated as an opportunity to prepare, not as evidence that financing risks have disappeared,” he said.

articles.title: Fitch highlights risk of U.S. sovereign rating downgrade as interest payments on developed market debt surpass $3.3 trillion - 富途牛牛
articles.summary: Fitch highlights risk of U.S. sovereign rating downgrade as interest payments on developed market debt surpass $3.3 trillion  富途牛牛
articles.full_text:
In fiscal year 2026, the U.S. federal budget deficit is projected to reach $1.99 trillion, up 12% year over year, while net interest payments are expected to surge past $1.05 trillion, hitting a record high. Fitch Ratings warns that if the budget deficit, the share of interest payments in government revenue, and the government debt-to-GDP ratio continue to deteriorate, and if no credible fiscal adjustment plan is put in place, the U.S. sovereign credit rating will face downward pressure. France and the United Kingdom are likewise under strain.
Against the backdrop of the U.S. federal deficit widening to $1.99 trillion and net interest payments reaching a record $1.05 trillion in fiscal year 2026, Fitch Ratings has explicitly warned that the U.S. sovereign rating faces the risk of a downgrade.
Data released by the U.S. Treasury Department on October 16 show that, for the fiscal year 2026 ending September 30, the federal government's budget deficit reached $1.99 trillion, up roughly 12% from the same period a year earlier. This marks the largest annual deficit since 2021 and the fourth consecutive year at this elevated level.
Rising U.S. Treasury yields have sent interest expenses soaring, becoming a key driver of the expanding fiscal deficit. In fiscal year 2026, the federal government's net interest outlays increased by $81.4 billion year over year, reaching a record $1.05 trillion and making interest payments one of the three largest categories of government spending.
Fitch Ratings projects that by year-end, total government debt in advanced economies will surpass $75 trillion. According to data from the Institute of International Finance (IIF), even before the latest wave of bond sell-offs, governments in wealthy countries were already paying more than $3.3 trillion annually in interest—exceeding global defense spending or the combined total of investments in artificial intelligence.
Fitch has designated the United States, France, and the United Kingdom as countries whose debt stability is under threat and whose sovereign ratings face downgrade risk, explicitly stating that if the three key indicators—high fiscal deficits, interest payments as a share of government revenue, and government debt as a share of GDP—continue to deteriorate, and if a credible medium-term fiscal adjustment plan remains absent, the U.S. sovereign rating will come under downward pressure.
Government bond issuance and tech giants' fundraising are creating a dual squeeze.
Brian Coulton, Chief Economist at Fitch Ratings, attributes the recent surge in bond yields to the combined effects of supply and demand. He noted:
The duration of the energy shock has exceeded earlier expectations, reshaping market perceptions of monetary policy and prompting central banks worldwide to remain vigilant about second-round inflationary effects.
Notably, not only are short- and medium-term bonds under pressure, but the yield on the 30-year ultra-long-term Treasury bond is also rising in tandem, while medium- to long-term inflation expectations have remained broadly stable. Brian Coulton stated:
This indicates that broader supply-and-demand factors are also at play.
Supply-side pressures stem first from the persistent expansion of fiscal deficits across governments. In its latest World Economic Outlook released in October, the International Monetary Fund noted that net borrowing by advanced economies worldwide will reach 5.2% of GDP this year, the highest level since 2021.
According to data from the U.S. Treasury Department, for the fiscal year 2026 ending September 30, the federal government's budget deficit reached $1.99 trillion, up roughly 12% year over year—the largest annual deficit since 2021 and the fourth consecutive year at a high level. Net interest payments increased by $81.4 billion year over year, hitting a record $1.05 trillion and becoming one of the government's three largest spending categories.
Meanwhile, large-scale fundraising by tech giants is competing with sovereign bonds for market capital. Brian Coulton notes:
Amid the AI investment boom, major tech‑cloud companies have begun raising substantial capital to fund data‑center and IT‑infrastructure projects, creating competition for funds in both the debt market and with sovereign bonds.
Goldman Sachs had projected that the five major hyperscale cloud service providers—Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle—would issue bonds totaling approximately $250 billion in 2026, with this figure rising further to $400 billion in 2027. Brian Coulton summarized:
Against a backdrop of rising investment demand and stagnant savings, this is putting upward pressure on real interest rates in the United States and globally.
The United States, France, and the United Kingdom face the greatest pressure, with the debt maturity structure emerging as a key variable.
Federico Barriga-Salazar, Director and Head of Western European Sovereign Ratings at Fitch Ratings, believes that rising financing costs are putting pressure on all developed markets, particularly those with high debt levels and large concentrations of bond maturities; France, the United States, and the United Kingdom are among the most affected.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva recently warned that advanced economies have become the "most egregious offenders" when it comes to debt. As debt-servicing costs continue to rise, fiscal space in many countries is further constrained, limiting their ability to provide support to households facing rising living costs.
A country's fiscal capacity to withstand shocks depends largely on the average remaining maturity of its outstanding debt. Federico Barriga-Salazar notes that the UK government's debt has an average remaining maturity of 13.4 years, while France's stands at 8.2 years, implying that any sharp rise in bond yields will be passed on to overall fiscal interest‑rate burdens gradually.
However, he also cautioned that France's short-term maturing debt stands at 15.9% of GDP, and should market financing conditions deteriorate, this would impose a short-term liquidity shock on the French fiscal position.
In response to concerns that turmoil in the French bond market could reignite the European debt crisis, Federico Barriga-Salazar offered a relatively cautious assessment. He emphasized that Europe has established multiple layers of institutional safeguards—namely the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), the Banking Union, and various support instruments deployed by the European Central Bank—designed precisely to prevent risk spillovers from escalating into a systemic crisis.
Deterioration in the three key indicators could trigger a downgrade of the sovereign rating.
Ed Parker, Global Head of Sovereign and Supranational Ratings at Fitch Ratings and Managing Director, clearly outlined the key signals that could trigger a downgrade in sovereign ratings: whether high fiscal deficits can be narrowed, whether the ratio of interest payments to fiscal revenue continues to rise, and whether the government debt-to-GDP ratio can stabilize.
He warned:
If these indicators continue to deteriorate and the government fails to present a credible medium-term fiscal adjustment plan, it could put downward pressure on the sovereign credit rating.
Fitch's report indicates that, among the world's ten largest advanced economies, the median yield on 10-year government bonds exceeds the average interest rate on outstanding debt by 161 basis points, making it increasingly difficult to reduce or even stabilize debt levels.
Ed Parker pointed out that government bonds generally have long maturities, and it will take time for rising bond yields to translate into an increase in the average effective interest rate on outstanding debt, thereby providing the government with a certain policy adjustment window. However, he also emphasized:
If the debt-to-GDP ratio rises rapidly, while lacking a credible fiscal framework and the political will to implement policies, it signals an increased risk to public‑debt sustainability.
Taking France as an example, Fitch's calculations indicate that, to keep its debt burden stable, the country would need to reduce its primary fiscal deficit from this year's projected 2.9% of GDP to 0.4% of GDP. Moreover, if real financing costs were to rise to current market yield levels, France would require an additional fiscal adjustment equivalent to roughly 3.1% of GDP.
Ed Parker stated that, for both the United States and France, "any further deterioration in public finances would serve as a sensitive trigger for a credit rating downgrade."
Editor/Liam

articles.title: Copper price falls as LME stocks edge higher and mine supply concerns ease - Mining.com
articles.summary: Copper price falls as LME stocks edge higher and mine supply concerns ease  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Copper prices fell on Monday as rising inventories and the end of a strike at a major Chilean mine eased supply concerns.
Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.4% at $14,342 a metric ton by 1600 GMT.
Available copper stocks in LME-registered warehouses rose to a two-month high of 147,450 tons after 8,225 tons of inflows into US warehouses, daily exchange data showed.
Copper inventories outside the US have declined in recent months as traders diverted shipments to the country ahead of potential tariffs on refined copper imports, helping prices to a record high of $14,875 a ton on September 10.
Deutsche Bank’s head of metals research, Daniel Ghali, said the threat of US tariffs is part of a broader strategic shift driven by national security concerns over concentrated critical minerals supply chains rather than a one-off policy risk.
Even if tariff concerns were removed, transportation costs and market friction would continue to discourage large-scale exports from the US, he added in a note.
Copper was the top choice for the industrial metal with the best outlook for higher prices, attendees at the LME seminar said on Monday. Tin was in second place followed by aluminium and nickel.
In top metals consumer China, meanwhile, economic growth bounced off three-year lows in the third quarter owing to higher exports. The country’s property market, however, remains in a downturn.
On the supply side, workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine ended a strike that began on October 7.
Among other LME metals, aluminium added 0.7% to $3,021.50 a ton. China’s primary aluminium production hit a record quarterly high over July to September as smelters maintained high operating rates despite a government-imposed capacity ceiling.
In other metals, zinc rose 0.8% to $3,721 a ton while lead edged up 0.3% to $1,894.50. An industry body expects a surplus in both of these markets in 2027.
Tin gained 1% to $50,860 and nickel rose by 1.3% to $15,555.
(Reporting by Polina Devitt; Editing by David Goodman and Diti Pujara)
