articles.title: Gold edges up as oil retreat lends support; Fed decision in focus - Kitco
articles.summary: Gold edges up as oil retreat lends support; Fed decision in focus  Kitco
articles.full_text:
Oct 19 (Reuters) - Gold prices edged higher on Monday as lower oil prices alleviated inflation concerns ahead of next week's Federal Reserve monetary policy meeting, where the central bank is widely expected to hold interest rates steady.
Spot gold rose 0.2% to $4,172.87 per ounce by 1109 GMT. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.3% to $4,193.30 per ounce
"Lower oil prices are easing pressure on the Fed, which is supportive for gold. What is notable is that gold is holding up even as the dollar strengthens, as demand for safe-haven assets is benefiting both," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
Oil prices slipped from a five-month high on Monday after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia that may lead to more Russian fuel exports.
The drop in oil prices eased some inflation concerns after strong US CPI and PPI readings last week, driven in part by a surge in gasoline costs.
Investors now await next week's Fed meeting and US PCE data, the central bank's preferred gauge of inflation.
"We expect the Fed to stay on hold this time, so the meeting itself may not be a major driver for gold. The key will be what the incoming inflation and labour-market data say about the path for rates," Staunovo added.
According to the CME's FedWatch Tool, opens new tab, traders are pricing in only a 15% chance of a rate hike this month, while expectations for a December increase remain high at 89%.
While gold is typically considered a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates reduce the appeal of the non-yielding asset.
Elsewhere, the European Central Bank is likely to raise interest rates by 25 basis points at least one more time this year to fight inflationary pressures, the International Monetary Fund said on Friday.
Among other metals, spot silver gained 1.2% to $57.6704 per ounce, platinum rose 1.3% to $1,652.22 per ounce and palladium climbed 2% to $1,134.25 per ounce.
Reporting by Vishak Mathew in Bengaluru; Editing by Leroy Leo

articles.summary: Pound To New Zealand Dollar Week-Ahead Forecast: RBNZ Bets Hinge On Inflation  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
The Pound-New Zealand Dollar could strengthen if UK inflation reinforces BoE hike bets, while softer New Zealand inflation may weigh on the Kiwi.
Trade in the Pound to New Zealand Dollar (GBP/NZD) exchange rate was uneven last week amid a fluctuating market mood.
At the time of writing, GBP/NZD was trading at around NZ$2.358. Almost unchanged from start of last week’s session.
DAILY RECAP:
The New Zealand dollar (NZD) tracked shifting risk appetite throughout the week, experiencing notable swings as investors reacted to geopolitical uncertainty, rising energy prices and changing expectations for US interest rates
After initially struggling amid concerns over renewed tensions in the Middle East, the ‘Kiwi’ was catapulted higher as a sharp correction in the US Dollar (USD) triggered a notable risk rally in the latter half of the session.
The New Zealand Dollar also benefited from comments by Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) Chief Economist Paul Conway, who signalled that further interest rate increases could be necessary to bring inflation under control.
The Pound (GBP) traded without strong conviction through the first half of last week’s session, as conflicting economic signals left investors hesitant.
Although the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its outlook for UK economic growth, gains were constrained by remarks from Bank of England (BoE) Chief Economist Huw Pill.
Pill, typically regarded as one of the more hawkish members of the Monetary Policy Committee, sought to rein in expectations for an aggressive tightening cycle, questioning market bets that the BoE would raise interest rates four times over the coming year.
The Pound found firmer footing later in the week, however, after the latest UK GDP figures revealed an unexpected expansion in August, overturning forecasts that the economy would contract.
Near-Term GBP/NZD Forecast: UK Inflation in the Spotlight
Looking ahead, the Pound to US Dollar exchange rate could gain ground this week as investors reacted to the latest UK consumer price index.
Forecasts point to inflation climbing to 3.4% in September. Such a reading could lend support to Sterling by reinforcing expectations that the BoE will start raising interest rates next month.
However, the latest UK labour market figures may limit the Pound’s advance. Unemployment is expected to have increased in August, potentially tempering optimism over the strength of the domestic economy.
Meanwhile, New Zealand’s own inflation figures will likely act as the primary catalyst for the ‘kiwi’ with NZD exchange rates likely to soften if an easing of price pressures in the third quarter dampens RBNZ rate hike expectations.

articles.full_text:
Summary
- The attacks in the Middle East continue
Oil prices have reversed higher in light of fresh reports about two separate Middle East strikes. WTI had traded down to $99.24 earlier and brent to $106.82, both after the US waived santions on Russian fuel.
That move now seems to have bought about 15 hours of lower oil prices and now crude is up on the day, with WTI at $103.13 and brent just above $110.
Two stories have driven the gains, the first is that the Iranian navy said the US attacked the Konarek naval base with "two light projectiles" early this morning and that wo solidiers were injured.
More recently, a pair of reports highlight that Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi Arabia in the past 48 hours, including strikes on the Yanbu oil facility owned by Aramco, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Ryiadh and Abha. Today, Saudi Arabia cancelled this year's 'Davos in the Desert' conference.
The next quesion is what will be the retaliation for the latest strikes on both sides. The US hadn't attacked Iran in seven weeks; Trump also said no attacks before the midterms. This one was characterized as small so perhaps it's ignored as Iran continues to focus on striking ships transiting Hormuz.
WTI crude oil daily:
Looking at the chart, oil has been climbing steadily higher in the past two weeks and is now within striking distance of the Sept 14 high of $104.95. We're getting very close to the point where a drop is too late to help Trump in the midterms so negotiations will be fruitless, despite a Qatari report today about new proposals.
Beyond the midterms, the calculus likely points to escalation, though at that point Republicans and Democrats may wish to sharpen their anti-war chops ahead of the 2028 election cycle. If Republicans suffer a rough defeat in the midterms, Congress could add pressure on Trump to exit Iran and find a way to make a deal. Alternatively, the US administration may simply conclude that the blockade on Iran and periodic strikes on shipping is a long-term strategy that will win.
What's more-concerning than the near-term chart is that if you look further out on the curve. October 2027 oil prices are at $83 and that's up $13 since the start of September and above the pre-war peak. That's the market doubting the endless promises from Trump that oil prices will "come crashing down".

articles.summary: Pound strengthens as Fed and Bank of England policy paths diverge  Crypto Briefing
articles.full_text:
The British pound has gained strength as differing economic outlooks between the Federal Reserve and the Bank of England are reported. The divergence in monetary policy expectations is influencing market perceptions, with the Fed taking a cautious approach to rate hikes while the Bank of England faces pressure from persistent inflation. This separation in central bank strategies appears to be lending support to the sterling’s recent advance, as markets reassess the likelihood of interest rate decisions by the Bank of England.
Key Takeaways
- The pound’s rise suggests market participants are reacting to the contrasting monetary policy indicators from the Fed and the Bank of England.
- Pricing suggests that the likelihood of a rate cut by the Bank of England in November has decreased, reflecting expectations of ongoing inflationary pressures.
- Current market activity shows a significant expectation for the Bank of England to increase rates by 25 basis points, consistent with recent inflation data and energy cost concerns.
What to Watch
The Bank of England’s upcoming policy meeting in November will be a focal point for market participants. Observers will be closely watching for any changes in inflation data and statements from key officials, such as Governor Andrew Bailey. Any shifts in the bank’s communication or economic indicators could further influence the market’s expectations of interest rate changes, potentially affecting the pound’s strength and market pricing for central bank actions.

articles.title: EUR/USD Edges Higher as Eurozone Growth Hopes Offset Hawkish Fed Concerns - InteractiveCrypto
articles.summary: EUR/USD Edges Higher as Eurozone Growth Hopes Offset Hawkish Fed Concerns  InteractiveCrypto
articles.full_text:
EUR/USD edged higher this week, closing at 1.1253 on October 16, 2026, up 0.4015% from 1.1208 the previous day. Among the five major pairs tracked here, that ranked as the third-largest absolute move of the session. In other words, the rise was meaningful enough to notice, but it was not a market-wide shock or a clear breakout on its own.
That distinction matters. The move was exactly in line with the median absolute move in the tracked universe, which suggests traders were responding to a familiar mix of macro expectations rather than a single dramatic catalyst. For EUR/USD, the current balance remains the same: modest support from Eurozone resilience on one side, and continued support for the dollar from a relatively hawkish Federal Reserve on the other.
Eurozone resilience is helping the euro, but only at the margin
The euro’s latest gain fits a broader idea that the Eurozone economy has held up better than some investors feared. When markets become a little more comfortable with regional growth, the euro tends to benefit because traders become less aggressive about pricing in weakness or policy easing.
Still, the price action argues for caution. Over the last 5 days, EUR/USD is up 0.26%, but over 20 days it is still down 1.28%. That gap shows a short-term rebound inside a softer medium-term trend rather than a fully established turn higher.
The pair’s position inside its recent range reinforces that point. The latest close of 1.12387 sits just 15.9% of the way from the 90-observation low of 1.11555 to the high of 1.16785. Put simply, EUR/USD has bounced, but it is still trading much closer to the lower end of its recent range than the upper end. That makes the current move look more like stabilization than a decisive recovery.
For readers trying to interpret the headline, this is the practical takeaway: optimism around Eurozone growth may be enough to stop the euro from sliding further for now, but the data in hand does not yet show a strong trend reversal.
The Fed is still limiting how far EUR/USD can run
On the other side of the pair, the US dollar remains supported by the idea that the Federal Reserve is not ready to turn clearly dovish. Even without a fresh shock, a cautious or hawkish Fed tends to keep US yields and dollar demand relatively firm, which caps upside in EUR/USD.
That helps explain why a positive day for the euro did not produce an outsized move. If the market believed the policy gap between the European Central Bank and the Fed was closing quickly, EUR/USD would likely be trading with more momentum than a 0.4015% daily rise and a 0.37% 20-day daily volatility backdrop suggest.
Instead, the pair is behaving like a market caught between two incomplete stories:
- the Eurozone is not weak enough to force a sharp repricing lower in the euro - the US outlook is not soft enough to knock the dollar decisively off its footing
That usually produces range trading, short bursts of direction, and quick reversals when incoming data fails to confirm a stronger narrative.
Why this move matters even if it is not exceptional
Because EUR/USD is the world’s most watched currency pair, even a modest move can matter beyond the trading desk.
For importers and exporters, a firmer euro slightly changes invoice economics. European companies buying dollar-priced goods face somewhat higher costs when the euro is weaker and a bit more relief when it strengthens. US firms selling into Europe may see the opposite effect when revenues are translated back into dollars.
For investors, the move can alter returns on unhedged positions. A US-based investor holding euro-denominated assets gets a small currency tailwind when EUR/USD rises. A euro-based investor with dollar exposure sees the reverse.
For travelers, the impact is simpler. A stronger euro modestly improves the purchasing power of Europeans spending in the US, while Americans heading to the Eurozone get slightly less value from each dollar.
None of those effects are dramatic after a one-day move of 0.4015%, but they become more noticeable if a series of similar sessions builds into a trend.
Context from the broader major-pair board
Relative performance also helps keep the move in perspective. AUD/USD rose 0.6946% and GBP/USD gained 0.6643%, both larger than EUR/USD’s advance. USD/JPY, by contrast, moved only 0.0253%, while USD/CAD fell 0.3238%.
That comparison suggests the euro was not the sole focus of the session. EUR/USD participated in a broader set of moves across major currencies, but it was not the standout. That is another reason to avoid overstating the significance of the latest rise.
For readers following the market day to day, this is useful context: the euro did strengthen, but the move looked more like part of a normal major-FX session than a singular repricing event.
Volatility remains relatively contained
The pair’s 20-day daily volatility stands at 0.37%, which is low enough to frame the latest move as active but still orderly. A market with contained volatility can still trend, but it usually needs repeated confirming signals to break out of a range.
That matters for businesses deciding whether to hedge immediately or wait, and for traders deciding whether to chase momentum. In a low-volatility environment, false starts are common. A one-day rise can fade quickly if the next round of inflation, growth, or central-bank commentary leans back toward the dollar.
What to watch next
The clearest watch point is whether EUR/USD can build on this rebound after spending the past 20 days in negative territory. The short-term gain of 0.26% over 5 days is encouraging for euro bulls, but it remains small relative to the 1.28% decline over 20 days.
That means the next phase matters more than the latest headline. If incoming Eurozone data continues to support the idea of resilience, the euro may keep recovering from the lower end of its recent range. If US inflation or Fed communication reinforces a higher-for-longer message, the dollar could reassert itself and keep EUR/USD pinned near recent lows.
A practical signal to monitor is whether the pair can move away from the lower portion of its recent range rather than merely bouncing inside it. Right now, with the latest close only 15.9% up from the recent low toward the recent high, the burden of proof is still on the upside.
For readers looking to place this move in a broader market framework, our guides to What is forex and Forex and CFD Brokers provide useful background. For those comparing trading access, platforms like eToro are one route traders use to follow major-pair moves such as EUR/USD.
Bottom line
EUR/USD’s rise to 1.1253 was real, but it was not extraordinary. The move matched the median absolute move across the tracked major pairs and ranked third out of five, which points to a normal but meaningful session rather than a decisive break.
The euro is getting some support from better growth sentiment, yet the dollar remains underpinned by Fed caution. Until one side of that balance clearly gives way, EUR/USD looks more like a pair trying to stabilize near the lower end of its recent range than one launching into a sustained new trend.

articles.title: Why Brent crude could hit $120 amid Iran war? What it means for India as analysts warn oil prices to remain volatile - Livemint
articles.summary: Why Brent crude could hit $120 amid Iran war? What it means for India as analysts warn oil prices to remain volatile  Livemint
articles.full_text:
Crude oil prices are likely to remain volatile in the coming week as stalled US-Iran negotiations, escalating tensions in West Asia and persistent supply risks keep global energy markets on edge, according to analysts cited by news agency PTI.
While measures to ease supply shortages could offer temporary relief, uncertainty over the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the threat of further attacks on energy infrastructure continue to underpin prices.
Monthly oil market reports from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and the International Energy Agency (IEA) will also be in focus.
Crude oil futures rose sharply over the past week as concerns over supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions outweighed hopes of an improvement in global availability.
On the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX), crude oil futures for November delivery climbed ₹566, or 6.4%, over the week to close at ₹9,394 per barrel.
In international markets, Brent crude futures for December delivery rose $5.14, or nearly 5%, to settle at $109.86 per barrel, touching the $110 mark on Friday.
Ajit Mishra, senior vice-president of research at Religare Broking, told PTI that the outlook remained cautiously bullish, with prices likely to respond more to geopolitical developments and actual supply disruptions than to headlines alone.
Recent declines in US crude inventories have added to the upward pressure. Mishra said a further escalation in geopolitical risks could push Brent crude towards $115-120 per barrel.
The Strait of Hormuz remains a major source of uncertainty for oil markets. Any disruption to shipments through the strategic waterway could further tighten global supplies and drive prices higher.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Tehran's proposal to reopen the strait within seven days remained on the table, according to Iranian media reports.
Iran submitted the proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response, but negotiations have stalled. Iran's security chief said last week that Washington had failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the waterway.
The lack of progress has left markets weighing the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough against the risk of further escalation and disruption to one of the world's most important oil transit routes.
Navneet Damani, head of research for commodities at Motilal Oswal Financial Services, told PTI that crude oil's muted response to bearish developments suggested that physical supply constraints were increasingly outweighing optimism over policy measures.
Releases from G7 strategic stockpiles, a US-Russia diesel arrangement and plans to ease sanctions on Moscow's shadow fleet had raised expectations of improved availability. However, these measures have failed to trigger a sustained decline in prices.
Logistical bottlenecks and an uneven recovery in supply continue to constrain crude availability.
The increase in West Asian exports in September was largely driven by Saudi Arabia, while vessel attacks, Houthi threats and limited capacity on alternative routes have left regional shipments vulnerable to further disruption.
Damani also cited stalled US-Iran negotiations, delayed Chinese crude arrivals and an estimated drawdown of 8 million barrels in US inventories as factors adding to supply concerns.
The IEA's warning of prolonged tightness in diesel supplies has added to concerns over the availability of refined petroleum products. Both the IEA and the US Energy Information Administration have projected a broader recovery in supplies only in 2027, subject to higher production and secure export routes.
The geopolitical outlook remains fluid amid concerns that the conflict in West Asia could widen further.
US President Donald Trump has said Washington was considering joining Saudi strikes against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen following an attack on Riyadh's international airport.
Any expansion of hostilities could increase the risk of attacks on commercial shipping and energy infrastructure, complicating efforts to restore stable oil flows.
Mishra said further escalation or damage to energy facilities in West Asia could push crude prices higher by increasing the geopolitical risk premium.
An executive order by Trump waiving key sanctions, restrictions and tariffs relating to Russia and Iran has offered temporary relief to major buyers of Russian oil, including India, amid rising energy prices.
However, the measures do not eliminate the risk of supply disruptions. Attacks on Russian energy infrastructure could still affect production and exports, leaving crude markets exposed to developments involving both Russia and West Asia.
For India, one of the world's major crude oil importers, a sustained rise in prices could increase the cost of energy imports and add pressure on domestic fuel prices and inflation.
Analysts said the market's direction would depend largely on whether geopolitical tensions translate into actual disruptions to production and shipments.

articles.title: Leveraged ETF losses of 200 billion won reignite controversy at FSS audit, with calls to 'block them at all costs' - 머니투데이
articles.summary: Leveraged ETF losses of 200 billion won reignite controversy at FSS audit, with calls to 'block them at all costs'  머니투데이
articles.full_text:
The controversy over single-stock leveraged ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds) is expected to reignite at the National Assembly audit of the Financial Supervisory Service scheduled for the 19th. The broad opposition camp is focusing on the fact that while retail investors incurred losses due to the introduction of single-stock leveraged ETFs, securities firms secured over 90 billion won in revenue through fees. It is anticipated that the point that this ultimately only fattened the pockets of securities firms will be intensely scrutinized. A debate over the responsibility of regulatory authorities is also expected to be unavoidable.
According to the financial investment industry on the 16th, the National Assembly’s Political Affairs Committee will conduct a National Assembly audit targeting the Financial Supervisory Service and others on the 19th. As with the National Assembly audit of the Financial Services Commission, the issue of policy responsibility for single-stock leveraged ETFs is expected to resurface.
During the Financial Services Commission audit, the main point of contention was responsibility for introducing the policy. At the Financial Supervisory Service audit, post-introduction side effects are predicted to be the focus of intense scrutiny. Single-stock leveraged ETFs were introduced with the goal of stabilizing exchange rates by attracting so-called retail investors in overseas stocks from foreign markets into the Korean market. Considering that various leveraged products are traded abroad, the intent was to expand investors’ choice of financial products and enhance the attractiveness of the Korean stock market.
As a result, retail investors flocked to single-stock leveraged ETFs, but most incurred losses. On the other hand, securities firms collected trading fee revenue in exchange for product brokerage, leading to criticism that they ultimately only fattened their own pockets.
According to data submitted by the Financial Supervisory Service to the office of People Power Party lawmaker Choi Eun-seok, the confirmed trading loss amount for retail investors related to single-stock leveraged and inverse ETPs (ETFs and ETNs) was found to be 232.42 billion won. This is based on aggregated data from 10 comprehensive financial investment businesses covering the period from the product launch on May 27 of last year to August 14 of last year.
Conversely, securities firms were found to have earned 93.1 billion won in entrusted trading fees over two months since the product launch. This figure was aggregated by the office of People Power Party lawmaker Kim Jae-seop based on data submitted by the Korea Financial Investment Association, covering the period from the listing of 16 single-stock leveraged ETFs for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix until the end of July last year.
Initially, there were discussions about the possibility of summoning securities firm CEOs to the National Assembly audit as witnesses, but all witness nominations failed to materialize.
Regulatory responsibility will also be questioned regarding Lee Chan-jin, head of the Financial Supervisory Service. In a regular press briefing in June last year, the head stated, "I regret not having stopped it even by lying down," referring to single-stock leveraged ETFs, which caused a stir. This was because it implied that financial authorities acknowledged that the policy introduction had minimal effects while side effects grew large. Consequently, at the Political Affairs Committee’s business report session in July last year, he apologized, saying, "I deeply feel the responsibility" and "We sincerely apologize."
Measures regarding margin investing (investing with debt) due to recent stock market volatility have also emerged as a major issue. As of the 15th last month, the scale of credit trading financing, which is the amount investors borrowed from securities firms to purchase stocks, reached 3274.98 billion won.
After the Financial Supervisory Service ordered securities firms to strengthen margin investing (investing with debt) management, the Korea Financial Investment Association released a plan to strengthen voluntary management of credit financing last month with 10 comprehensive financial investment businesses, including Mirae Asset Securities and Korea Investment & Securities. The plan includes reducing the scale of credit extension from 100% to within 90% of securities firms’ own capital, and managing the proportion of credit financing for specific stocks within 15%. The Financial Supervisory Service plans to strengthen monitoring to ensure that securities firms comply with the voluntary management measures.

articles.title: Lagarde calls for fiscal discipline as energy inflation strains Europe - finchannel
articles.summary: Lagarde calls for fiscal discipline as energy inflation strains Europe  finchannel
articles.full_text:
The FINANCIAL — Christine Lagarde called for fiscal discipline on Saturday, Oct. 17, urging governments to keep energy relief temporary and focused on those who need it as Europe confronts renewed inflation and higher borrowing costs. The European Central Bank president said heavily indebted countries should restore room in their budgets through consolidation, revised spending priorities and more efficient public finances.
In her statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee, Lagarde argued for a measured monetary response to an energy shock too large to ignore. She also said higher long-term interest rates would slow growth and limit the transmission of energy costs into other prices more than the ECB had projected in September.
The statement did not announce a new interest-rate decision. It set out the bank’s assessment of an economy facing pressure on prices alongside tighter financing conditions, with governments also being asked to preserve room to respond to future shocks.
Inflation rises across the euro area
The immediate inflation figures show the scale of the renewed pressure. Euro-area consumer prices were 3.8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, up from a 3.2 percent annual increase in August, according to Eurostat’s October 16 release. Prices increased 0.6 percent from August to September.
Energy prices rose 18.9 percent over the year, compared with 14.3 percent in August. Services inflation increased to 3.2 percent from 3 percent. The measure excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco rose to 2.5 percent from 2.4 percent.
The regional average conceals national differences. Annual inflation was 3.3 percent in Germany, 3.4 percent in France, 4.2 percent in Italy and 5 percent in Spain. A year earlier, euro-area inflation had been 2.2 percent. These are European harmonized consumer-price measures, covering a different geography from the United States’ consumer price index.
The ECB’s September rate increase
The ECB’s most recent policy action cited in Lagarde’s statement was a quarter-point increase in September. Its September 10 decision raised all three key rates by 25 basis points, taking effect on September 16. The deposit rate became 2.5 percent, the main refinancing rate 2.65 percent and the marginal lending rate 2.9 percent.
The decision retained the bank’s 2 percent medium-term inflation target and a meeting-by-meeting approach to policy. The ECB said it was not committing itself to a particular path for rates. Its assessment combines the inflation outlook and associated risks, underlying price dynamics and the transmission of monetary policy through the economy.
The bank also continued to let its asset-purchase portfolios decline by not reinvesting principal from maturing securities. It retained its Transmission Protection Instrument, which can address unwarranted, disorderly market movements that seriously threaten the transmission of monetary policy across euro-area countries.
Growth forecasts depend on a fading energy shock
The September ECB staff projections envisaged euro-area growth of 0.9 percent in 2026, 1.4 percent in 2027 and 1.5 percent in 2028. Those figures are forecasts, rather than completed annual growth results. The estimates for 2026 and 2027 had been raised by 0.1 and 0.2 percentage points, respectively, from the June projections.
Staff expected domestic demand to benefit from recovering real incomes and a resilient labor market as energy inflation eased. Infrastructure and defense spending, especially in Germany, and investment related to artificial intelligence were also expected to support activity over the projection period.
The export outlook was more qualified. Strengthening foreign demand was expected to help, but competitiveness problems would continue to constrain exports. The euro area was also expected to benefit less than some other economies from global AI demand because its AI goods sector is smaller.
Irish multinational activity adds another complication to the regional figures. A measure adjusting for that volatility put projected growth at 1.2 percent in both 2026 and 2027, followed by 1.4 percent in 2028.
The cost of protecting households
The International Monetary Fund’s October World Economic Outlook describes a global economy still expanding but facing an uneven recovery. It projects growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, with global headline inflation at 4.7 percent and 4.1 percent, respectively. The estimates use information available through October 1.
Energy-importing economies outside technology supply chains face the most difficult outlook, the fund said. It identified further conflict, renewed trade tensions, fiscal vulnerabilities and a reassessment of AI expectations among the downside risks. Stronger AI investment and productivity gains, or sustained easing of geopolitical and trade tensions, could improve the outlook.
Its research on cost-of-living crises favors temporary, targeted income transfers that preserve price signals. Measures that suppress prices can require three to 22 times as many fiscal resources as targeted, temporary transfers, the report found. That range is a research finding across the episodes examined, rather than a fixed cost ratio for every government program.
Debt service narrows governments’ options
The IMF’s fiscal researchers have separately described the strain from higher sovereign borrowing costs. The average yield on 10-year government bonds across the Group of Seven rose by more than one percentage point between February and September, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, according to an IMF fiscal-policy article published October 15.
The fund projects global public debt above 100 percent of global gross domestic product by 2030. It expects the effective average interest cost of government financing to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent in 2031.
For the United States, the article projects interest payments increasing from about 2.8 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7 percent in 2031. Those are projected future payments, rather than a statement of today’s federal interest bill.
Refinancing at shorter maturities can transmit higher policy rates to government budgets more quickly. The researchers also put the global primary deficit at about 3.3 percent of GDP in 2026, compared with roughly 2.6 percent needed to stabilize the debt ratio that year.
Financial markets retain vulnerabilities
The IMF’s October Global Financial Stability Report finds that markets have remained resilient, supported by growth and corporate earnings, while financial risks remain elevated. It identifies a possible correction in AI-related assets, a shock to sovereign bond yields and increasingly sophisticated cyber threats among potential triggers for turmoil.
The report describes the global banking system as broadly resilient, while acknowledging pockets of weaker banks. Among nonbank institutions, liquidity mismatches at insurers and pension funds and leverage in private credit could amplify stress.
Hedge funds hold about $13 trillion in assets globally, more than three times their 2013 level, according to the report. They can support liquidity and price discovery in normal markets. During stress, however, leveraged positions, crowded trades and correlated redemptions can force simultaneous asset sales, with losses or funding strains spreading to other institutions.
American technology finance draws scrutiny
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s October Financial Stability Review documents another connection between the AI boom and credit markets. Technology-related companies accounted for nearly 30 percent of U.S. investment-grade corporate bond issuance in the first half of 2026. That is a share of new issuance, rather than of all outstanding corporate debt.
AI firms are increasingly using corporate bonds, private credit, bank loans and asset-backed financing to fund large projects, the RBA said. It described aggregate leverage as contained and balance sheets as generally healthy, with large technology companies often supported by other revenue streams, including advertising and e-commerce.
Risks differ across the industry. Some data-center developers and cloud-infrastructure providers have weaker balance sheets or concentrated customer bases. Guarantees from larger companies and financing through special-purpose vehicles can support construction, while creating contingent exposures and links among developers, lenders and infrastructure investors. The RBA warned that opaque arrangements can make the industry’s financial exposures harder to assess.
Did euro-area prices fall in September?
No. Eurostat reported a 0.6 percent monthly increase and a 3.8 percent annual increase. A slower inflation rate would mean prices rising more slowly, rather than necessarily falling.

articles.title: Financial Authorities Ignore Warnings, Launch Single-Stock Leveraged Products - 조선일보
articles.summary: Financial Authorities Ignore Warnings, Launch Single-Stock Leveraged Products  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Seven months before the launch of single-stock leveraged products that allow betting twice the daily volatility of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares, a commissioned research report by the Financial Supervisory Service was confirmed to contain warnings that "domestic introduction should be approached cautiously." The reasons included concerns over investor losses, increased stock market volatility, and the trend of strengthened regulations in other countries such as the U.S.
However, single-stock leveraged products were rapidly launched just over four months after discussions on their introduction began in earnest in January this year. After the KOSPI plummeted in June–July, these products were identified domestically and internationally as a major factor exacerbating market volatility. Critics argue that financial authorities rushed the launch without sufficiently assessing the risks, despite prior warnings about the need for caution in domestic introduction.
◇Ignoring warnings, rushed launch, and post-crash measures
According to data received by Representative Park Dae-chul’s office, a member of the National Policy Committee of the People Power Party, from the FSS on the 16th, the Korea Capital Market Institute submitted a 151-page report titled *‘Analysis of Successful Cases in Overseas Asset Management Industry and Implications’* to the FSS in October last year. The report noted the possibility of the U.S. strengthening regulations on single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and pointed out that "Korea should be cautious in pursuing policies that explicitly allow these (single-stock leveraged ETFs), as it could face global regulatory consistency issues in the future."
Despite these prior warnings, the introduction of single-stock leveraged products began in earnest at the start of this year. Kim Yong-beom, then Policy Secretary of Cheong Wa Dae, said in a January media interview, "I asked the Financial Services Commission, ‘If it’s possible on NASDAQ, why can’t we do it?'" The FSC announced a legislative notice for amendments to the Enforcement Decree of the Capital Markets Act at the end of January and revised regulations on April 28 to allow domestic launches . Just one month later, on May 27, 16 products based on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were listed.
At the time, the stock market was heating up on the back of a semiconductor boom. President Lee Jae Myung stated during his first-year press conference on June 8 that stock prices "seemed to have risen faster than expected," but added, "I still think they are slightly undervalued." On the 19th of the same month, the KOSPI broke through the 9,300 mark during trading hours but began a sharp decline afterward. Concerns grew that trading in single-stock leveraged products could further amplify fluctuations in Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix stock prices. Lee Chan-jin, Governor of the Financial Supervisory Service, even remarked, "I regret that we should have done whatever it took to block it." As criticism poured in, the FSC raised the minimum deposit requirement for these products from 10 million Korean won to 30 million Korean won, among other measures to raise the entry barrier. The average daily trading volume, which reached 11.86 trillion Korean won in July, dropped to around 560 billion Korean won this month.
◇Warnings in the U.S.…discussions on sales regulations
The researcher revealed in the FSS commissioned report that while single-stock leveraged ETFs exist in the U.S., they were not actively permitted by financial authorities, who instead warned about investment risks. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) simplified the launch process for general ETFs in 2019 but excluded leveraged products. However, the following year, new regulations on derivatives allowed leveraged ETFs to use the simplified process. As a result, even single-stock leveraged ETFs were launched without separate SEC approval. The report assessed this as an "unintended consequence."
However, U.S. financial authorities strongly warned about the risks. In 2021, then-SEC Chairman Gary Gensler stated that just because leveraged ETFs are listed "does not mean they are suitable for all investors." He also expressed concerns that rapid market changes could pose risks to the financial system. Later, the SEC’s Office of Investor Education and Advocacy warned that single-stock leveraged ETFs are "highly unsuitable for ordinary individual investors with long-term investment strategies."
The report also introduced the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority’s (FINRA) move in 2022 to seek public comments. The inquiry asked whether securities firms should more strictly verify investors’ risk tolerance when selling complex products like leveraged ETFs. The report assessed this as "a concrete move to effectively restrict individual investors’ access."
Representative Park Dae-chul stated, "Were financial authorities prioritizing product launches over investor protection?" and emphasized, "They must clearly explain how they reviewed investment risks at the time."

articles.summary: FX Summary: 25bp Fed Hike Bets, Oil Shock, Tech Selloff  FinanceFeeds
articles.full_text:
Global markets face inflation pressures, central bank divergences, Middle East energy supply disruptions, and tech sector turbulence affecting risk assets.
Persistent Inflation Pressures and Central Bank Policy Divergence
Recent economic data has confirmed that the inflation tightness building since the summer is far from transient. Hotter-than-expected US Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Producer Price Index (PPI) reports have reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will implement a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at its December 9 meeting, following an anticipated pause on October 28. This hawkish outlook stands in sharp contrast to other central bank trajectories. In Canada, headline inflation rose to 3.1% year-over-year in September, missing forecasts and pushing institutions like Scotiabank and the Bank of Montreal to call for a preemptive rate hike to narrow the policy gap with the United States. Meanwhile, the Swiss National Bank maintains its policy rate at 0% while its inflation stays within the 0% to 2% range, further cementing the divergence between the Greenback and its global peers.
Middle East Geopolitics and Energy Supply Disruptions
Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have served as a primary catalyst for global energy shocks and subsequent pricing volatility. Ongoing conflicts in the Persian Gulf—highlighted by Houthi attacks on the Shaybah oilfield and Yanbu Aramco site, alongside disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz—have kept supply risks elevated and fed directly into broader global price data. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude initially rallied past $99.00 on unconfirmed reports of US strikes and restricted maritime traffic. However, prices later retreated after US President Donald Trump signed an order temporarily waiving specific Russia sanctions and tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian crude, providing alternative supply pathways for nations like India and temporarily easing upward pressures.
Tech Sector Volatility and Risk-Asset Sentiment Shifts
Global equity markets experienced significant turbulence driven by a synchronized correction in technology stocks and broader risk-off sentiment. The tech-heavy Nasdaq suffered steep losses, exacerbated heavily by severe financial distress and soaring debt yields at AI infrastructure provider CoreWeave. Rather than dragging down the broader currency, this tech sector unwind prompted foreign investors to rotate out of equities and back into safe-haven US Treasuries and government bonds. Consequently, the shifting risk appetite has influenced broader safe-haven flows, capping the upside for alternative non-yielding assets like Gold while reinforcing the defensive appeal of the US Dollar.

articles.title: French 10-Year Bond Yield Nears 5% as Stocks, Bonds and Currency Sell Off - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: French 10-Year Bond Yield Nears 5% as Stocks, Bonds and Currency Sell Off  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
French financial markets suffered a broad selloff on Monday, with bonds, equities and the euro all falling in tandem. A wave of large-scale protests combined with uncertain prospects for fiscal consolidation have sharply heightened investor concerns over French sovereign debt risk, with the 10-year government bond yield briefly approaching the 5% mark.
As of press time, the French 10-year government bond yield had surged 15 basis points in a single day to 4.93%, the largest one-day increase in nearly a month. Meanwhile, the German 10-year yield rose 4 basis points to 3.45%, and the France-Germany spread widened to 146 basis points, a two-week high. The Italian 10-year yield also climbed 11 basis points to 4.58%, as markets worry that volatility in French bonds could spread to other highly indebted eurozone economies.
France's CAC 40 fell 1.5%, a steeper decline than the roughly 1% drop in the pan-European Stoxx 600, making it the worst performer among major European markets. Bank stocks bore the brunt, with BNP Paribas and Industrial Bank each down about 3%. The retail sector also came under pressure, with Carrefour shares falling 1.8%; its chief executive said the company would suffer losses in the tens of millions of euros from protest-related damage. The euro fell 0.2% to 0.3% against the dollar, pound and yen, the weakest performer among Group of 10 currencies.
The premium on French sovereign credit default swaps rose 5 basis points to about 82 basis points, the worst-performing sovereign CDS in Europe on the day. Moody's will review France's sovereign credit rating on Friday, and given its negative outlook, a downgrade is seen as the more likely next step. Moody's currently rates France one notch higher than Fitch and S&P Global.
Fiscal consolidation meets political resistance
At the heart of the market turmoil is eroding investor confidence in France's ability to effectively reduce its fiscal deficit. Weak economic growth and a steadily swelling debt burden had already weighed on France's finances, and the social unrest has further clouded the outlook for budget reform.
The protests, which began over the rising cost of living and deteriorating school conditions, spread rapidly across France over the weekend, accompanied by violence and looting. Several stores were ransacked in Paris and other cities, and the historic city hall in Limoges, a city in west-central France, was severely damaged by fire during the unrest. French President Emmanuel Macron later described the weekend's events as a "disgrace and an outrage." According to preliminary figures, more than 2,000 people were arrested across France and hundreds of businesses suffered serious property damage. France's central government has asked some local authorities to impose curfews, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has not ruled out declaring a state of emergency.
"The market move follows the large-scale protests and signals that reform expectations are fading," said Hank Calenti, a global markets strategist at SMBC. The reforms he referred to cover both deficit reduction and pension reform.
Investors widely believe France must advance budget legislation as quickly as possible to rebuild confidence in its fiscal trajectory. However, political maneuvering ahead of next year's presidential election may complicate that process further. Calenti also noted that the shock has spread across the eurozone, with reform prospects dimming in multiple markets.
French politicians are debating the 2027 budget. The government's bill includes 43 billion euros (approximately $48.2 billion) in deficit-reduction measures. Reaching a compromise in a deeply divided parliament was already difficult, and it may become even harder with only six months until the presidential election. Investment manager Ninety One warned on Monday that if the government fails to pass the 2027 budget, France's deficit next year could exceed 6% of gross domestic product, more than double the EU's 3% ceiling.
Widening spreads and rating risk
The France-Germany 10-year bond spread has widened to 146 basis points, the highest in two weeks. Although it has retreated from a peak of about 160 basis points in early October, market moves suggest the spread risks returning to those highs. In early October, the French 10-year yield briefly touched 4.99%, the highest since 2002, and this week the yield is once again approaching that key level.
"France today is simultaneously facing a social crisis, an immigration crisis, an energy crisis, an economic crisis and a fiscal crisis," said Louis-Vincent Gave of Gavekal Research. He added that nothing that happened over the weekend appeared to point toward anything that would support the euro or push French bond yields lower.
"While violent protests do not represent the vast majority of the population, the weekend's developments still highlight the difficult balance the government faces between reassuring the public and reassuring the markets," said Eric Liem, a strategist at Commerzbank. The bank's analysts believe a Moody's downgrade would merely bring it into line with other rating agencies, so the negative impact on spreads may be fairly limited.
Analysts also noted that the growing participation of hedge funds in the French bond market is increasing market fragility, a risk that has drawn close attention from regulators.
Fiscal bind and shrinking policy room
The structure of French public spending makes fiscal adjustment harder. Compared with 1974, when France last achieved a balanced budget, spending on public services such as security, justice and education has changed little as a share of GDP, while pension-related spending has risen by about 6.5 percentage points, with nearly a third of France's education budget going toward pension outlays.
Charlotte de Montpellier, senior economist for France at ING, said that if France wants to genuinely improve its debt dynamics, it needs to reform a pension system whose costs are significantly higher than in other countries, but such a policy is highly unpopular politically.
Elias Hilmer, a market economist at Capital Economics, said French OATs are consistently the focus of concentrated selling in the current sovereign debt selloff. He expects the spread between French and German 10-year yields to widen from about 140 basis points currently to 200 basis points by the end of 2027, while spreads for most other eurozone countries relative to Germany may narrow over the same period.
There are also limits to how much support the European Central Bank can provide. If the rise in French bond yields stems mainly from substantive concerns about its public finances rather than a malfunction in the broader eurozone bond market, it may be harder for the ECB to intervene directly.
The French government thus faces pressure from both the streets and the bond market: expanding fiscal spending could ease some social pressure but may further weaken market confidence in debt sustainability, while accelerating fiscal consolidation touches highly sensitive areas such as pensions, public services and household incomes. As the 2027 budget and presidential election approach, investors are pricing France's ability to execute fiscal policy ever more directly into government bond yields and the France-Germany spread.

articles.title: IMF Warns AI Correction Could Spark Financial Turmoil - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: IMF Warns AI Correction Could Spark Financial Turmoil  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
The IMF's October 2026 Global Financial Stability Report names an AI-driven market correction as one of three risks capable of triggering widespread financial turmoil. The other two are rising sovereign-bond yields and cyberattacks.
Markets remain resilient, and the IMF is not predicting imminent collapse. Its own stress tests indicate that banks could withstand a severe downturn, though the fund is clearly telling regulators to pay closer attention before vulnerabilities grow more serious.
How a Correction Could Cascade
A single earnings disappointment, amplified by debt and concentrated exposure, could move fast.
Substantial AI investment is clustered among a relatively small number of companies and financing channels. If profits fail to meet ambitious expectations, asset prices could correct sharply, and the damage would not stay neatly contained.
According to the IMF briefing, a faltering in AI monetization could trigger a damaging feedback loop. Falling equity values weaken borrower balance sheets, make debt harder to service, and erode the future revenue projections that supported the original spending.
Circular financing adds another layer of opacity. AI companies can simultaneously act as investors, financiers, suppliers, and customers for one another, making it genuinely difficult to assess how much independent demand actually exists. The IMF flags this as a concern; its published material does not yet quantify the exposure.
The Bank for International Settlements raises a related concern from a different angle. AI investment is increasingly debt-funded and structurally complex, spanning hyperscalers, data-center developers, and nonbank lenders.
According to Reuters reporting on the BIS analysis, the five largest hyperscalers were on pace to spend more than $1 trillion on AI capital expenditure across 2025 and 2026 combined. The BIS draws comparisons to earlier boom-and-bust cycles, in which high expectations of transformative productivity gains preceded a sharp reversal in investment when those returns did not arrive.
Supply-side bottlenecks add further exposure. Firms that have committed heavily to scarce capacity in power generation, electricity grids, data centers, and memory chips could be especially vulnerable if AI demand disappoints, according to the BIS.
Bonds, Banks, and Bytes
Three separate risks share one uncomfortable trait: they can reinforce each other.
Rising sovereign-bond yields are the second named risk. Higher yields push up borrowing costs for governments, companies, and households.

articles.title: Central banks may soon become boiling frogs - OMFIF
articles.summary: Central banks may soon become boiling frogs  OMFIF
articles.full_text:
According to the old parable, a frog placed in tepid water that is heating slowly lingers until it is too late and boils to death. Is the parable applicable to the future of independent central banks?
Central bank independence is essential for achieving sound inflation outcomes. It is a global public good, absolutely worth preserving. But even if central banks stress that they are responsible for achieving their mandates, they do not operate in a vacuum and cannot achieve their objectives alone. Monetary and fiscal policies are interconnected, though that is no reason to compromise central bank independence.
Fiscal policy in particular is a key determinant of economic outcomes. Economies are often institutionally structured to separate monetary and fiscal policy – central banks are responsible for monetary policy; Treasuries and parliaments for budgets.
But large fiscal deficits and debt can boost aggregate demand and inflation, causing central banks to hike interest rates. They can push up yields and boost debt-servicing costs, creating political and fiscal pressures for central banks to cut rates, engage in yield curve control or bond buying, or undertake financial repression to limit debt-servicing costs. As President Donald Trump put it in a 2025 Truth Social message – ‘Fed should cut Rates by 3 Points. Very Low Inflation. One Trillion Dollars a year would be saved!!!’
Higher unsustainable rates due to poor economic policy or heightened rollover risks can create financial market instability, compelling central banks to inject liquidity to steady financial conditions despite poor fundamentals that aren’t being fixed. Political uncertainties, inflation persistence and unsustainable debt dynamics can drive up the term premium and crowd out private investment, undermining efficiency.
Withstanding external pressure
Whether central banks can withstand pressures from political and fiscal authorities in such circumstances is not a given, as history has amply shown. President Richard Nixon’s pressure on the Arthur Burns Federal Reserve is a preeminent example.
As a general proposition, central banks avoid commenting on fiscal policy. They may briefly mention that fiscal policy is unsustainable. But they often argue that speaking about fiscal stabilisation policy is beyond their remit, notwithstanding monetary policy impacts. They further aver that doing so may embolden politicians to speak about monetary policy. It’s better to stay in their lane. Of course, politicians are not shy anyway about flaunting their views on monetary policy.
In the US, Trump’s crusade against Fed independence undoubtedly compounds Fed hesitancy to utter the word ‘fiscal’, even though US fiscal policy is reckless.
But fiscal and financial dominance are undeniably rising realities with the potential to undermine central bank independence. Can the Fed in the face of sharply rising yields, continued supply shocks and Trump breathing down its neck, seeking to overhaul the Fed Board, ignore the pressures on the institution? Can the European Central Bank really just say that France must solve its fiscal problems when France’s bond market is the largest in Europe and the potential for contagion is great? Can one really believe that the Bank of Japan’s slow march to normalisation has not been influenced by Japan’s already high debt and concerns over the potential for soaring debt-servicing costs?
Of course, in the US’s case, the Fed could simply ignore such pressures, adjusting monetary policy strictly in line with its mandate. The same applies for the ECB and BoJ. But is that so easy and realistic?
A duty to the public
Central banks should be economic consciences for the nation. They are staffed with top-flight officials and first-rate economists who understand the interplay between fiscal dynamics and monetary policy and economic outcomes. As I have argued previously, the fiscal chickens are coming home to roost.
Their first and highest priority must be to fulfill mandates and bring inflation back to target. But central banks owe it to society to somewhat step out of their comfort zones, educate the public, responsibly speak truth to power and call out fiscal woes more explicitly, if nothing else making clear the ramifications for monetary policy and short and long rates. They certainly have no qualms about speaking on artificial intelligence and monetary policy implications. Why not fiscal policy?
It is perhaps a poisoned chalice. Even if doing so provokes political firestorms, especially in the US, speaking up may ultimately help protect independence. The alternative is that central banks run the risk of being overwhelmed by fiscal shortcomings, losing independence and ending up like the boiling frog.
Mark Sobel is Vice Chair and Chief Economist of OMFIF.
Join OMFIF on 21 October for a lecture with Andrew Bailey, governor of the Bank of England, on central bank independence.

articles.full_text:
Markets and Economy Are we there yet? Bull market may have more miles
Key takeaways
- Some credit markets became more selective, but stress hasn't broadened to all areas of the credit markets. Companies with stronger balance sheets and cash flows may continue to access capital.
- Recent inflation data has been uncomfortably strong, but longer-term inflation expectations have remained relatively contained, and concerns about confidence in US assets may be limited.
- The indicators we watch have suggested that the ride may be slowing, but that the bull market doesn’t appear to be coming to an end, and may not be for a while.
We recently drove our oldest daughter to college. Ten hours in the car gives you plenty of time to think. At some point, I remembered the question I used to ask my parents on long road trips.
“Are we there yet?”
“No.”
“When will we be there?”
“Not for a while.”
“Are we getting closer?”
“Well, of course we are.”
That exchange feels surprisingly relevant for investors today.
It has been a long, positive ride for the US stock market.1 History offers some warning signs on how things have tended to end. Too much borrowing. Too much inflation. Too much monetary policy tightening. Credit spreads widen. Investors paying up for default protection. Cyclical stocks selling off. Treasury yields falling as investors seek safety. The US dollar strengthening.
That’s a reasonable recap of the news flow over the past few weeks,2 but it doesn’t necessarily mean that the bull market ride is ending.
Credit stress has risen, but not broadened
Start with leverage. The rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure has increasingly depended on debt financing, and the bond market has started distinguishing among borrowers.3 CoreWeave is the latest example. Yields on some of its unsecured debt have climbed to roughly 15%, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has risen sharply.4 Since June, wider credit spreads have accounted for roughly half of the increase in high-yield borrowing costs.5 The rise may no longer simply be a rates story. It increasingly appears to reflect concerns about credit quality.
That shouldn’t be dismissed. But neither should it automatically be interpreted as the end of the AI investment cycle, in my view. Demand for computing capacity has remained substantial. I believe the more likely consequence may be that capital becomes more discriminating. Companies with stronger balance sheets, visible cash flows, contractual support, and better financing structures will likely continue to have access to capital, in my opinion. Weaker, more leveraged projects may find that capital becomes prohibitively expensive or unavailable. Importantly, spreads in the higher quality parts of the bond market remained relatively tight, suggesting that the stresses haven’t broadened across credit markets.6 That’s what credit markets are supposed to do. They differentiate.
Leverage is one thing. Leverage combined with Federal Reserve (Fed) tightening is another. As rates rise, financing has gotten more expensive, and the economy has tended to slow. That doesn’t mean the journey is ending, but it may be a sign that we’re getting closer.
Markets appear prepared for tighter policy
That brings us to inflation. Recent inflation data have been uncomfortably strong.7 But the bond market rallied in response to the strong Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index releases.8 That suggests to me that markets had already priced in the rate hikes and are now preparing for tighter policy to slow economic activity. Importantly, longer-term inflation expectations have remained relatively contained.9 The recent rally in US Treasuries and resilience of the US dollar10 suggests to me concerns about confidence in US assets may be limited. That seems like a signal that the recent rise in yields may never have been primarily about concerns over fiscal sustainability.
Journey continues, quality matters
None of this means investors should ignore what’s happening. Cycles generally haven’t ended without warning. Financing became more expensive. Credit became more selective. Weakness appeared in the more speculative corners of the market.
Those mile markers matter.
That also has implications for how we invest. As the credit markets become more discerning and the economy slows, we favor higher-quality credit and more defensive sectors of the stock market. We also watch for signs of a reacceleration in economic activity, which could occur with a resolution of the oil shocks, and/or a rally in bond prices.
So, are we there yet?
No, I don’t think so.
Are we getting closer?
Sure. Every mile of a long journey gets you closer to the destination.
The indicators we watch suggest the ride may have slowed, but I don’t believe the bull market is over yet, and it may not be for a while.

articles.title: Korea’s FSS chief says leveraged ETF review was rushed, blame still unassigned - Cryptopolitan
articles.summary: Korea’s FSS chief says leveraged ETF review was rushed, blame still unassigned  Cryptopolitan
articles.full_text:
- FSS chief Lee Chan-jin told a National Assembly audit on Monday that the review of single-stock leveraged ETFs was rushed to hit a launch date.
- Lee is the third senior Korean regulator to concede fault after products tied to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix triggered trillions of won in retail losses.
- No official has been held responsible, and the FSC admitted it never estimated whether the “bring money home” rationale would work.
South Korea’s top financial supervisor has admitted to lawmakers that regulators pushed single-stock leveraged ETFs through review to meet a launch date.
The Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) chief Lee Chan-jin is now the third senior official to admit fault for products that cost retail investors trillions of won.
What did the FSS chief admit to?
The Financial Supervisory Service chief Lee Chan-jin admitted at the National Assembly’s Political Affairs Committee audit on Monday that the FSS finished its work with single-stock leveraged products before the exchange was done, instead of allowing the ETF listing to clear a Korea Exchange preliminary review first.
Even after this admission, it is still unclear who ordered the funds to be sold. Critics have named Kim Yong-beom, the former presidential policy chief; Lee Eog-weon, chairman of the Financial Services Commission; and Lee Chan-jin himself.
People Power Party lawmaker Park Dae-chul asked Lee if the steps had ever been done in reverse order before, and his response was that regulators had checked and it seemed this was the first time.
Lee said the speed was due to a deadline. After the FSC announced a listing schedule in mid-April, he said that the regulators “moved quickly through the review” in order to keep up.
May 27, which the FSC set as the launch date, was also the day that 16 funds went on sale with the aim to rise or fall by double the daily move of Samsung Electronics (KRX; 005930) or SK Hynix (KRX; 000660) shares.
The elections were held one week later, on June 3. Opposition lawmakers have repeatedly said the launch was timed to come just before the vote.
Lee said at a June 22 briefing that he felt he should have blocked the launch and that the products appeared to have “only fattened securities firms.”
On October 8, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon apologized at his own audit, saying he “deeply regret[s] the various losses, concerns, and damages that have resulted.”
A market note from Citi’s Mohamed Apabhai, head of Asia-Pacific trading strategy, put Korean retail losses at roughly $38.7 billion, or 58 trillion won, by late July.
The FSC chairman dismissed a separate 54 trillion won ($36.5 billion) figure from an overseas bank as unofficial, but the FSS’s own data confirmed 2.3242 trillion won ($1.57 billion) in realized trading losses at 10 financial investment firms between the May 27 launch and August 14.
Did the FSC anticipate retail losses?
The Finance Ministry, the Financial Services Commission (FSC), and the Bank of Korea all told lawmaker Kim Sang-hoon’s office that they never calculated how much the funds would reduce money leaving Korea or increase investment at home. Yet that was the FSC’s main argument when it first proposed the change on January 30.
The Cabinet approved the rule on April 21 through an enforcement decree, so the National Assembly never voted on it.
Within weeks, trading got out of control. On July 16, regulators stopped new funds from being listed. From July 31, they raised the minimum cash needed to trade the funds from 10 million won (about $6,750) to 30 million won ($20,250). Trading then dropped about 97% from its June peak.
Cryptopolitan previously reported that Korean traders have moved their money abroad in order to find leverage that domestic rules do not allow, using KORU-linked perpetual futures on Binance, Bybit, OKX, and KuCoin that can run to 150 times the Kospi’s daily swing.
Tiger Research, working with Chainalysis, estimated about 700 trillion won left domestic exchanges between 2021 and 2026. Licensed Korean crypto exchanges shed 35% of their won deposits in the first half of 2026.

articles.title: Gold Prices Edge Higher as Fed Rate Outlook and Indian Economic Impact Remain in Focus - Trade Brains
articles.summary: Gold Prices Edge Higher as Fed Rate Outlook and Indian Economic Impact Remain in Focus  Trade Brains
articles.full_text:
On October 19, gold prices increased due to market assessments of the interest rate expectations before the next policy decision by the US Federal Reserve. Spot gold prices increased by 0.2% to stand at $4,171.65 per ounce, and US gold futures for December delivery increased by 0.26% to $4,191.90 per ounce, according to Reuters.
The price increase was attributed to low crude oil prices which helped ease inflation worries, hence reducing the probability of an even tighter monetary policy from the Federal Reserve. Safe-haven demand for gold continued to prop up gold prices amidst market uncertainties.
International gold prices are especially significant for Indian investors since a large proportion of the gold consumed is imported into India.
Factors Influencing Gold Prices
1. US Federal Reserve Interest Rate Projections: Investor attention is now fixed on the future course of policy and data from the Federal Reserve. As gold does not pay any interest, it becomes less popular when rates and bond yields are higher. On the other hand, the anticipation of falling rates may favor gold.
2. Price of Crude Oil and Inflation: The falling price of oil made investors feel secure about the threat of inflation from the rising cost of oil. Yet, crude oil price movements might affect the gold price.
3. US Dollar and Bond Yields: Gold prices are sensitive to movements in the US dollar and government bond yields. A stronger dollar can make gold more expensive for buyers using other currencies, while rising yields can reduce the appeal of non-interest-bearing assets.
For India, a weaker rupee can add to the domestic cost of imported gold, even when international prices remain unchanged.
4. Safe-Haven Demand: Investors often turn to gold during periods of geopolitical tension and economic uncertainty. Concerns about global growth, financial-market volatility and currency movements may continue to influence demand for the metal.
How Gold Prices Affect the Indian Economy
1. Rise in Cost of Imports and Trade Deficit: India sources most of the gold used domestically, thus making bullion one of the significant components of India's import bill. An increase in international prices may increase the cost of sourcing the same amount of gold, thereby contributing towards an increase in the country's trade deficit, assuming there are no changes in export income and other imports.
Nevertheless, the overall influence will depend on the total amount of gold imported. Recent information revealed that India's gold imports dropped 81.3% year-on-year to $1.8 billion in September 2026, which helped cut the merchandise trade deficit to approximately $30.2 billion.
2. Pressure on the Currency and Foreign Exchange: To buy gold from abroad, a country will require paying in foreign currency, mainly US dollar. Increased cost of imports may increase the dollar demand and put pressure on the country's currency, besides other factors such as high oil imports and capital flows out of India.
The weakening of the country's currency in itself may result in increased costs for imported gold in India. There is a likely feedback loop between the weakening of currency and price of bullion.

articles.summary: SBI Research urges tax clarity on G-Secs, ECB rules to deepen domestic borrowing markets  A2Z Taxcorp LLP
articles.full_text:
SBI Research has called for greater tax clarity on government securities (G-secs) and clearer rules for external commercial borrowings (ECBs), saying further policy measures could deepen domestic borrowing avenues and help support capital flows amid persistent pressure on India’s balance of payments.
In its Ecowrap report dated October 15, the research arm of State Bank of India said the rupee could remain in appreciating territory, but global financial turbulence and continuing capital-account deficits leave little room for complacency. It said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had taken steps to stabilise market conditions, while the government now needs to address structural frictions that may affect investment and funding decisions.
SBI Research said greater clarity on taxation relating to G-secs, ECB rules and AI policy could help deepen domestic borrowing avenues and support capital flows.
Policy clarity and borrowing options
The report did not detail specific tax changes or proposed amendments to ECB rules. Its broader recommendation is that policy uncertainty should be reduced to improve the environment for domestic borrowing and capital inflows. Clearer rules could help businesses and investors assess funding options, although the report did not quantify the likely effect of any changes.
SBI Research also called for a credible, time-bound roadmap for artificial intelligence covering data governance, accountability, compliance and infrastructure. It said predictable rules would be important to attract investment into India’s AI ecosystem as competition for technology-related capital intensifies.
Capital-account pressures
The report highlighted a change in India’s balance-of-payments position. While earlier episodes of sharp rupee depreciation were largely associated with pressure on the current account, capital-account deficits have become persistent since December 2024, it said. SBI Research argued that managing the rupee now requires attention to vulnerabilities in both accounts.
Combined overseas direct investment debt and equity outflows rose to $27.2 billion in FY25 and $27.8 billion in FY26, compared with $13.4 billion and $13.7 billion in the preceding two financial years, respectively. The report also urged closer scrutiny of non-essential overseas remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme to conserve foreign exchange.
Global bond-market conditions add to the uncertainty. The US 10-year Treasury yield briefly crossed 5.32% on October 14 after higher-than-expected US inflation data, before easing to around 5.19%. India’s 10-year government bond yield stood at about 7.38%, and SBI Research said it could touch 7.6%.
The report said policy action on taxation, ECB rules, overseas investment and AI could help strengthen capital flows. These are recommendations from SBI Research, rather than announced government measures.

articles.title: Economist sees 2% inflation by end of 2027, challenging market rate bets - Mortgage Professional America
articles.summary: Economist sees 2% inflation by end of 2027, challenging market rate bets  Mortgage Professional America
articles.full_text:
Why a spike in the January energy price cap could derail the 2027 inflation path
UK inflation could return to the Bank of England’s 2% target by the end of 2027, with interest rates falling from current levels, according to Darren Winder, head of Lazarus Economics and Strategy.
Winder made the prediction at the Brightstar Specialist Lending Expo 2026 at the London Stadium in early October. It runs against the current trend. UK CPI inflation rose to 3.1% in August, from 2.9% in July. The Bank of England voted 6-3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% in September, with three members preferring a rise to 4%.
“That’s the main prediction from today – that I come back here in 12 months’ time and we’re on track for 2% inflation,” he said. “If we’re on track for 2% inflation in 12 months’ time, interest rates will be lower than they are today.”
The outcome depends on energy prices. If oil falls from around $100 towards $80 during 2027 while gas stays near current levels, Winder said base effects should bring inflation back to 2% by the end of the year.
Energy price cap is the near-term test
Winder predicted the Government would step in to limit a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January. Without intervention, he warned, the Bank of England could forecast inflation approaching 4%, potentially pushing up market expectations for interest rates.
Ofgem raised the cap 4% to £1,723 on 1 October. Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16% rise to about £1,999 in January. The Government has not committed to specific support ahead of the 28 October Budget.
Challenging market pricing
Winder said financial markets currently point to rates close to 5% by the end of 2027. Mortgage One’s analysis of SONIA futures on 12 October implied about 4.9% by October 2027.
He said: “The market currently thinks interest rates are going to be nearly 5% by the end of 2027. I think it’s just for the birds.”
He argued that energy volatility, rather than domestic pressure, has driven much of the movement in inflation. Private-sector wage growth of around 3% and productivity growth of 1% imply unit labour costs rising about 2%, he said. ONS data put private-sector regular pay growth at 2.8% in the three months to June. Core CPI held at 2.6% in August.
Winder said: “Underlying inflationary pressures have clearly been easing, even though headline inflation is going up.”
Growth, saving and the case for cuts
Winder said annual growth had doubled over the past 12 months, from around 0.75% to 1.5%. The ONS put second-quarter growth at 1.4% on a year earlier.
“The growth rate of the economy factually has doubled in the last 12 months,” he said. “So it’s definitely getting there. It’s not there yet. Being there is 2%.”
Stronger household spending would be key to lifting growth, he said, with UK households saving around 9% to 10% of take-home income. The ONS estimated the saving ratio at 8.8% in the second quarter. Winder estimated that each one percentage point fall in the ratio could generate an additional £20 billion of consumer spending.
He said: “To me, the argument for getting interest rates down is to discourage saving more than it is to encourage borrowing.”
For advisers, the debate bears on client conversations about mortgage fixes, cash holdings and fixed-income allocation. Winder’s view contrasts with a split Monetary Policy Committee, and several data points arrive soon. CPI for September is due on 21 October, the Budget on 28 October, and the Bank’s next rate decision on 5 November.
