articles.title: Gold, silver, platinum, and palladium rebound; platinum main contract rises for two consecutive days; precious metals sector strengthens; spot silver trading overall sluggish [SMM Flash] - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: Gold, silver, platinum, and palladium rebound; platinum main contract rises for two consecutive days; precious metals sector strengthens; spot silver trading overall sluggish [SMM Flash]  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
SMM, October 19:
On October 19, gold, silver, platinum, and palladium rebounded collectively, and the A-share precious metals sector moved higher. The main drivers were Fed Chairman Warsh's remarks at the IMF annual meeting that he would not prejudge the October rate decision, prompting the market to lower the probability of a rate hike this month; combined with the previous oversold conditions in precious metals, short covering, and safe-haven support from Middle East geopolitics and US Treasury fiscal risks. Platinum and palladium additionally benefited from improved expectations for automotive catalysts and the hydrogen energy industry. As of 13:59 on October 19, COMEX gold rose 0.57% to $4,204.9/oz; SHFE gold main contract rose 0.42% to 902.56 yuan/g; COMEX silver rose 0.99% to $57.875/oz; SHFE silver main contract rose 1.09% to 14,040 yuan/kg; silver T+D rose 0.68% to 13,998 yuan/kg. In addition, the platinum main futures contract rose 1.92% to 405.85 yuan/g, and the palladium main contract rose 0.28% to 269.8 yuan/g.
Equities: As of the close on October 19, the precious metals sector rose 0.97%. Among individual stocks, Chifeng Gold rose 3.74%, and Shandong Gold, Western Gold, Zhongjin Gold, and Shanjin International were among the top gainers.
Spot market
On October 19, the SMM #1 silver morning ex-factory reference average price edged up from the previous trading day.
In the spot market, trading sentiment was poor today. On one hand, overall end-user purchasing sentiment was subdued. After silver prices stabilized following last week's sharp decline, large-volume transactions were already concentrated in the middle and latter part of the week. With silver prices rebounding slightly today, downstream buyers mostly turned to a wait-and-see stance. On the other hand, in early trading, the basis between TD and the SHFE 2612 contract widened slightly, trading around 35-45 yuan/kg. Suppliers quoted at relatively high levels, with early quotes in Shanghai concentrated at a discount of 30 yuan/kg against the SHFE 2612 contract, reflecting strong reluctance to sell. The wide gap between buyers' and sellers' quotes and psychological price levels led to poor actual transactions, which were mainly concentrated near parity with TD, with some national-standard cargoes at slight discounts.
Overall, macro bullish drivers were limited, and futures lacked momentum for a rebound. In the spot market, end-user wait-and-see sentiment remained strong, and the tug-of-war between suppliers holding prices firm and downstream buyers pushing for lower prices intensified, leaving overall trading sluggish.
On October 19, spot platinum extended the previous trading day's gains and continued to edge up.
In spot trading, mainstream quotations for platinum ingots from suppliers were around parity to a premium of 1 yuan/g against the PT2612 contract. As available platinum ingot supply in the market tightened, the spread in supplier quotations widened. Meanwhile, the price gap between platinum ingots and platinum powder was relatively large. Some suppliers reported that platinum ingot transactions generally carried a small premium against the GFEX contract, and downstream acceptance of spot premium quotations for platinum ingots improved, while transactions for platinum powder near parity faced resistance. Overall, the platinum spot market showed clear divergence today, with overall trading volumes normal.
Views from various parties
Regarding the future trend of precious metals, some institutions hold the following views:
Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, said: "Gold prices edged up at the start of this week. From an inflation perspective, softer oil prices have had a positive impact on gold prices. In the short term, if oil prices fall steadily, or if yields show a more pronounced decline, that would be the most favorable catalyst for gold prices, as both would ease market concerns about inflation and rate hikes." (Jin10 Data APP)
Hamad Hussain, climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, judged on October 16 that gold prices may trend lower for the rest of the year. He cited two reasons: the US Fed continuing to raise rates, and concerns about the end of the AI boom ultimately proving temporary. This means his view on gold prices involves both interest rates and the outlook for the AI boom. Bart Melek, global head of commodity strategy at TD Securities, said gold remains rangebound and biased toward the lower end of the support zone, mainly because there is still considerable uncertainty about the US Fed's next move. (Jin10 Data APP)
CITIC Securities research report noted that on gold prices, first, ETF and central bank gold purchases may have already lifted the bottom of gold prices; second, the outlook for gold prices still has positive conditions. If the US-Iran conflict eases before the US midterm elections, improved oil price expectations will create a foreseeable window for easing market tightening expectations, and the rise in US Treasury yields may moderate. From both the liquidity perspective (reduced futures selling) and the liquidity expectations perspective (continued ETF buying), this would be conducive to a recovery in gold prices. On the gold sector, looking downward, referencing the bottom gold price of $4,000/oz at end-June 2026, we estimate the gold sector PE bottomed at around 15x. At the current assumption of $4,200/oz, the sector's 2026/2027 PE is 15x/12x, and the valuation bottom is expected to be verified again. Looking upward, gold stocks usually rebound ahead of gold prices, similar to the July period when gold prices consolidated at lows, but the CITIC Gold Index has already rebounded more than 20% from its bottom, so if current gold prices stabilize, that would be an important signal for a rebound in the gold sector.
Sharon Ding, head of China basic materials research at UBS, said most of the bad news facing gold has already been priced in by the market. She said that since early September, gold prices have fallen about 5% as persistent inflation concerns reignited expectations of further US Fed rate hikes. However, she believes gold prices now already reflect a significant hawkish repricing. She noted that this headwind may begin to ease as market expectations for a US Fed rate hike in October diminish. "If upcoming data no longer support further upward revisions to the expected policy path, we believe there is more room for gold prices to stabilize," she added. She also said that a continued pullback in US Treasury yields could strengthen the case for a gold recovery. (Jin10 Data APP)
Strategists at State Street Global Advisors said in a report that the structural factors driving the gold bull market appear to remain intact. These factors include record government debt levels, strong physical gold demand from central banks and China's retail market, and heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty. The strategists said rising interest rates could further increase debt servicing costs for major economies, exacerbating fiscal imbalances. This year, the premium on domestic gold prices in China has surged sharply; despite higher gold prices, consumer gold imports in the first eight months still hit a record high of 1,141 mt. The strategists maintained their previous base-case forecast, expecting gold prices to reach $4,750-5,500/oz by the end of Q1 2027.
Saxo Bank analysts said: "Gold price action underscores the ongoing tug-of-war between macro traders and technical traders. On one hand, traders are selling gold due to rising funding costs and a stronger US dollar; on the other hand, investors are seeking to hedge against the fiscal risks that rising debt and borrowing costs may bring." (Jin10 Data APP)
The World Gold Council reported that global gold ETFs attracted $10 billion of inflows in September, pushing Q3 inflows to a record $31 billion, led by funds listed in Europe and North America. Despite lower gold prices, global gold holdings still increased by 67 mt to a record 4,256 mt, while total assets under management fell 7% QoQ to $574 billion. At the country and regional level, record Q3 inflows were led by the US, followed by strong contributions from UK-listed funds. The UK recorded its strongest quarter ever, helping Europe reach the same milestone at the regional level.
Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey, heads of the commodities team at ING, said gold prices edged up on Tuesday. Lower oil prices and a stronger bond market eased inflation concerns and reduced market expectations for further rate hikes. Meanwhile, continued central bank gold buying provided support for gold prices. World Gold Council data shows that central banks are still net buyers of gold, with long-term reserve diversification remaining the main driver. Data show that central banks globally continued to be net buyers of gold in August, adding 39 mt, bringing total purchases so far this year to 170 mt. Poland and Uzbekistan each added 8 mt. Türkiye returned to being a net gold buyer in August, buying 3 mt after three consecutive months of net selling. Other buyers included Kazakhstan, the Czech Republic, Bolivia, and Ghana. Russia reduced its gold holdings by 6 mt. The latest data show that despite high gold prices, official-sector gold demand remains resilient. Central banks' continued gold purchases are driven mainly by long-term reserve diversification goals rather than short-term market fluctuations. With Poland and several emerging-market central banks continuing to add gold, official-sector demand is likely to remain an important support for the gold market in the coming months.
HSBC previously lowered its gold price forecast, citing expectations of further US interest-rate hikes and the possibility that rising oil prices could pressure gold in the near term. However, the bank believes the long-term factors supporting gold prices remain intact. HSBC now expects gold to average $4,490/oz in 2026,

articles.title: Stocks rebound into key tech earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week - TradingView
articles.summary: Stocks rebound into key tech earnings: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week  TradingView
articles.full_text:
Bitcoin (BTC) starts the third week of October at $82,000 as crypto and stock markets begin a tentative rebound.
Key points:
- South Korea’s KOSPI Composite Index gained nearly 1.8% on Monday after last week’s tech-driven losses.
- Markets have priced out two further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve in 2026, seeing 75% odds of only one 25-basis-point hike by the end of the year.
- Bitcoin delivered a weekly close below key local support after the Coinbase Premium Index hit -0.14, its lowest level since late June.
Asia leads equities bounce ahead of tech earnings
A lighter week of US macro data prints will shift the market’s attention to corporate earnings as stocks rebound from last week’s sell-off. Some 15% of S&P 500 companies are due to report third-quarter earnings figures this week, including SpaceX on Tuesday and Tesla and Meta on Wednesday.
Tech-stock performance remains in focus after a major drawdown last week that began with South Korean markets. The KOSPI Composite Index lost 2.8% on Oct. 12 before dropping to the week’s low of 5,455 on Thursday, bringing the week-to-date losses temporarily to 17%.
KOSPI Composite Index one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Contagion spread to neighboring Asian markets before US equities began to weaken later in the week. The S&P 500 index finished Friday down 2% for the week.
As in early August, tech stocks saw considerable sell-side pressure amid concerns over AI expenditure plans and the associated debt obligations. In Korea, the threat of competition in semiconductor manufacturing from China exacerbated the downturn.
Warnings of a “Black Monday” event on global stock markets spread through social media over the weekend. The panic, which coincided with the 39th anniversary of the 1987 Black Monday crash, appeared misplaced, with KOSPI gaining 1.8% on Monday and S&P 500 futures 0.7% higher at the time of writing.
S&P 500 futures one-day chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Commenting on the disconnect between public sentiment and market performance, market commentator The Kobeissi Letter suggested that stocks should outperform based on investor demand. Persistent high US inflation and a global energy crisis have positioned equities for a surge on any potential signs of conditions improving.
“All while the AI Revolution continues to accelerate and many large-cap technology stocks become cheaper on a forward earnings basis, even as their stock prices rise. And in the background, the demand for asset ownership is historically robust,” it summarized in analysis last week.
Kobeissi noted that while tech giants led S&P 500 strength, 80% of index stocks are trading at least 10% below all-time highs.
Fed rate-hike bets cool despite inflation data overshoot
Ahead of the Federal Reserve’s next decision on interest-rate changes on Oct. 28, markets have tempered their expectations on policy tightening.
Data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool shows 85% odds of rates staying within their current 3.75-4.00% range in October. The Fed’s December meeting, meanwhile, carries just 11% odds of a further pause. Instead, markets see a 75% chance of a 25-basis-point hike, with a 50-basis-point move attracting 13% odds.
Fed target-rate probabilities (screenshot). Source: CME Group
In a discussion with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva last week, Fed chair Kevin Warsh avoided any hints of forward guidance on policy, reinforcing a pledge made at the Jackson Hole economic symposium in August.
“I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” he said.
Markets, however, interpreted the lack of information as a dovish signal, doubling down on the Fed hiking rates just once more before 2027.
Adopting a cautionary tone, meanwhile, market commentator Mosaic Asset Company saw inflation trends forcing the Fed to avoid easing off, keeping a crypto and risk-asset headwind in place.
“While investors expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady at its next meeting later this month, a growing inflation problem will keep favoring tighter monetary policy,” it wrote in analysis on Sunday.
The September print of the US Producer Price Index (PPI) released last week showed the ongoing impact of the Middle East crisis on fuel prices. PPI delivered its largest month-on-month increase since March 2022 at 1.7%.
“Half of the September increase in the index for final demand goods can be traced to prices for gasoline, which jumped 20.3%,” the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported.
Fuel also accounted for more than half of the September increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which beat expectations by 0.1% to hit 3.7% year-on-year.
BTC price analysis sees more $80,000 support retests
Bitcoin price action completed a weekly candle close below a key support zone of interest between $82,500 and $82,800.
The weekly close came in at $82,000, a move that crypto trader and analyst Rekt Capital warned could spark further retests of the $80,000 mark in the future.
“Such a Weekly Close would position Bitcoin for a potential bearish retest of ~$82500 into new resistance. And if that bearish retest occurs successfully then it could set price up for a drop below $80k within the next few weeks,” he wrote in analysis on X.
BTCUSD one-week chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Previously, Cointelegraph reported on September’s local high near $87,000 now hosting multiple resistance components, including the 2026 yearly open and its 20-month simple moving average (SMA).
In its latest market overview, onchain analytics platform CryptoQuant flagged declining US investor demand as a reemerging BTC price headwind this month. The Coinbase Premium Index, which measures the difference in price between Coinbase’s and Binance’s BTCUSDT pairs, fell to -0.141 on Oct. 18, its lowest levels since June 30.
“This reading is particularly significant. If the index remains in negative territory, it could indicate insufficient demand to absorb selling pressure, potentially increasing the likelihood of a continued price correction in the short term,” CryptoQuant commented.
Coinbase Premium Index. Source: CryptoQuant
The lack of demand contrasts with BTCUSD holding gains made since the end of June, having bounced from new multiyear lows under $58,000 on July 1.

articles.title: ECB rate decision Oct 29: what it means for crypto - CryptoTicker
articles.summary: ECB rate decision Oct 29: what it means for crypto  CryptoTicker
articles.full_text:
Which topics should we dive deeper into?
Select what genuinely interests you. Your picks feed directly into our editorial planning.
On Thursday, October 29, 2026, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank decides on euro area interest rates. The decision falls on the second day of the meeting, after which ECB President Christine Lagarde steps in front of the press. For your crypto portfolio this ECB rate decision matters for a reason that has little to do with the price on the day: the risk-free rate in euros now sits above the yield Ethereum staking delivers. Hold crypto and from this autumn you are no longer comparing against zero but against 2.5 percent.
This piece sets the date in context: where the rates stand today, why the central bank raised them at all, what a further step would mean for the price, for staking yields and for leveraged positions, and which points can be settled calmly in the ten days before the meeting. You will not find price forecasts for October 29 here. Anyone telling you how Bitcoin reacts to a decision nobody yet knows is guessing.
The Governing Council of the European Central Bank meets on October 28 and 29
The meeting calendar of the European Central Bank lists October 28 as day one of the monetary policy meeting in Frankfurt and October 29 as day two, followed by the press conference. That is the usual sequence: deliberation starts on Wednesday, the decisions and their reasoning come on Thursday. The decision is published in the early afternoon Central European Time, with the press conference following a good half hour later.
What matters for planning is the date after it. The next monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council is not in the calendar until December 16 and 17, 2026. Whatever is decided on October 29 therefore holds for around seven weeks. There is normally no interim decision; the central bank departs from that only in severe market disruption.
Deposit rate 2.5 percent: where the policy rates have stood since September 16
The ECB steers the money market through three rates. The most important is the deposit facility rate, the rate banks receive for overnight deposits with the Eurosystem. Since the decision of September 10, 2026, effective from September 16, the central bank's official rate table carries these values:
- Deposit facility: 2.50 percent. The rate that overnight money and short-term euro deposits take their bearings from.
- Main refinancing operations: 2.65 percent. The rate at which banks borrow weekly against collateral.
- Marginal lending facility: 2.90 percent. The overnight credit rate, the ceiling of the corridor.
The path to those levels explains why the subject counts right now. In June 2025 the deposit rate stood at 2.00 percent, the trough of the easing cycle. On June 17, 2026 the ECB lifted it to 2.25 percent, and on September 16 to 2.50 percent. Two increases in one year, after years of falling rates: since the summer of 2026 the euro area has been in a tightening cycle again, not in a phase of cuts.
Inflation at 3.8 percent: the reason for September's rate step
Price developments supply the reasoning. On October 16 Eurostat confirmed the annual euro area inflation rate for September 2026 at 3.8 percent, after 3.2 percent in August. That is the highest reading since September 2023 and sits well above the two percent target the central bank has set itself.
The rise comes almost entirely from one direction. Energy grew 18.9 percent more expensive within a year and so accounted for the bulk of the jump; without that rise in energy prices the rate would sit close to target. Core inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, by contrast, edged up only slightly to 2.5 percent. For Germany, Eurostat reports 3.3 percent.
That breakdown is decisive for assessing the date. A central bank can treat inflation driven mostly by energy prices differently from inflation that has settled into wages and services. Energy prices act with a lag and can fall back just as quickly. Whether the Governing Council adds another step on October 29 or waits hangs on precisely that question.
Fed on the 28th, ECB on October 29: two rate decisions in 24 hours
The week carries a peculiarity that often gets lost in European calendars. The US Federal Reserve meets on October 27 and 28 according to its own meeting calendar, the ECB on October 28 and 29. About a day lies between the two decisions.
For the crypto market the order carries weight. The Fed decides first, and the crypto market trades in US dollars: Bitcoin dominance stood at 60.2 percent on October 19, with total market capitalisation at around $2.77 trillion. If a marked move runs through the market on the evening of October 28, it very probably originates in Washington rather than Frankfurt. The ECB decision lands the following day on a market that has already priced the Fed in.
In practice that means anyone planning an order or a savings plan execution around those days should reckon with two jolts rather than one. And anyone seeing a large move on Thursday should check first whether it has anything to do with the ECB at all.
ECB rate decision and crypto: the three channels the policy rate works through
The link between monetary policy and cryptocurrencies runs through three channels, and none of them is magic.
The price of money
A higher policy rate makes credit more expensive. Companies and households have less free money, and some of it would otherwise have flowed into risky assets. Crypto sits well down that order of preference, behind equities and bonds. It shows up in inflows from companies and funds, not in a single day's price.
The alternative without price risk
As long as overnight money paid nothing, holding Bitcoin cost no forgone interest. At a deposit rate of 2.50 percent that changes. Any asset delivering no running income now competes with a rate you receive without price risk. The same applies to Bitcoin and to gold. Specialists call it opportunity cost.
The euro-dollar exchange rate
If euro area rates rise faster than US rates, the euro tends to firm against the dollar. Bitcoin is quoted in US dollars. A firmer euro lowers the euro price of a coin even when the dollar quote does not move. On October 19 Bitcoin stood at around $82,700 and around €73,700; Ethereum at about $2,428 and €2,164. Count in euros, then, and you never see exactly the same move as an observer watching the dollar quote.
Staking yield against the risk-free rate: 2.20 against 2.50 percent
This is where the rate decision gets concrete for crypto investors. The yield from Ethereum staking currently sits below the ECB deposit rate. DefiLlama data show an annual yield of around 2.20 percent for Lido, the largest liquid staking provider, on roughly $23.4 billion of deposited capital, and around 1.98 percent for Rocket Pool. Our own measurement of October 18 came to 2.21 percent and set it against the ECB rate of 2.50 percent; the assessment is in our analysis of the staking yield below the ECB rate.
The comparison limps in one place by design, and that belongs in the picture. A staking yield accrues in ether and carries the cryptocurrency's full price risk, plus smart contract risk and, at some providers, a withdrawal period. The central bank's deposit rate, by contrast, is interest on euro balances. Two yields in two different currencies with two different risks cannot be set cleanly against each other.
Something shifts nonetheless. Hold ether solely for the staking yield and above a certain rate level the argument weakens. If the ECB raises again on October 29, that gap widens. Which platform pays out how much and which lock-up periods apply is shown in our comparison of staking platforms; a look at the actual net yield after fees pays off before any renewal.
Bitcoin on rate days: leverage and liquidation in a thin order book
Dates with a fixed time create a pattern of their own. Ahead of publication many traders pull their orders out of the book, because nobody wants to stand on the wrong side of a surprise. The order book thins out, and in a thin book the same order size moves the price further than usual.
For leveraged positions that is the dangerous part. A liquidation is the forced closing of a position when the margin no longer suffices. It is triggered by the brief spike in between, not by the closing price. Trade with leverage and you check the distance between the current price and your own liquidation price before days like these, then decide deliberately whether that buffer is enough for a rate decision.
Without leverage the subject is calmer. A spot holding survives a swing of a few percent without consequence, as long as you do not have to sell.
Euro balances, stablecoins and overnight deposits between the dates
A rising deposit rate also affects the money sitting on an exchange between two purchases. Three routes are open, and they differ in one point that is easily overlooked.
A euro balance in a German overnight deposit account earns interest, and the level follows the central bank's deposit rate at some remove. A euro balance on a crypto exchange as a rule earns nothing; it sits there ready as a means of payment. Euro stablecoins, in turn, are tokenised euro claims; the interest income from the backing reserves accrues to the issuer, not to the holder.
At a deposit rate near zero that difference was immaterial. At 2.50 percent, a larger balance sitting unremunerated on a trading platform for months costs noticeable money. Leave longer gaps between purchases and you move the part you do not need back to the bank account. Which venues offer a euro deposit without the detour through a stablecoin is set out in our crypto exchange comparison.

articles.summary: Pound To Canadian Dollar Week-Ahead Forecast: Oil Prices Support Loonie  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
The Pound-Canadian Dollar rate could remain volatile as UK jobs and inflation data shape BoE expectations, while Canadian CPI may influence the Loonie.
Trade in the Pound to Canadian Dollar (GBP/CAD) exchange rate was volatile last week, amid mixed domestic catalysts and fluctuating commodity prices.
At the time of writing, the GBP/CAD exchange rate traded at CA$1.8869. Almost unchanged from the start of last week’s session.
DAILY RECAP:
The Pound (GBP) traded unevenly during the first half of last week, with a mix of positive economic news and cautious comments from the Bank of England shaping market sentiment.
An upgrade to the UK’s growth outlook from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) provided some encouragement, with its forecast for 2026 raised from 1% to 1.3%.
However, the Pound faced headwinds after Bank of England (BoE) Chief Economist Huw Pill challenged expectations of an aggressive tightening cycle.
While acknowledging the need to contain inflation, Pill questioned whether the central bank would deliver four interest rate increases over the next year.
Momentum shifted in the Pound’s favour during the latter half of the week, when UK GDP figures unexpectedly showed the economy expanding in August.
The stronger-than-forecast reading reinforced expectations of a November rate hike from the BoE, while offering Chancellor John Healey some welcome relief ahead of his forthcoming Budget.
The Canadian dollar (CAD) remained closely tied to movements in global oil prices this week.
This saw the commodity-linked currency stage a notable mid-week rebound as crude prices climbed amid renewed concerns over disruptions to global energy supplies.
However, a subsequent pullback in oil prices, coupled with some cautious remarks from Bank of Canada (BoC) Governor Tiff Macklem, led the ‘Loonie’ to relinquish the bulk of these gains by the end of the session.
Near-Term GBP/CAD Forecast: Stream of UK Data to Drive Sterling
A packed calendar of UK economic data could bring renewed volatility to the Pound to Canadian Dollar (GBP/CAD) exchange rate this week.
Investors will be paying particular attention to the latest employment and inflation figures, both of which will help shape expectations ahead of the BoE’s November interest rate decision.
In the meantime, Canada’s own consumer price index could lift the ‘Loonie’ if a rise in inflation is seen as placing more pressure on the Bank of Canada to tighten monetary policy.

articles.title: Jio Platforms IPO: Rs 2.5 lakh crore demand for Rs 8,110 crore anchor book - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: Jio Platforms IPO: Rs 2.5 lakh crore demand for Rs 8,110 crore anchor book  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: Jio Platforms' initial public offering has attracted institutional demand of about Rs 2.5 lakh crore, with global asset managers, sovereign wealth funds, domestic mutual funds and insurers among investors seeking a stake in the Reliance Industries subsidiary ahead of its stock market debut.
The company's Rs 8,110-crore anchor book drew demand of more than 30 times the amount on offer, according to figures provided for the transaction, sources privy to the development said.
The scale of interest highlights the institutional appetite for the telecom and digital services business as it prepares for a separate listing.
Among the global investment firms putting offers for the anchor book are BlackRock, Capital Group, Fidelity Investments, T. Rowe Price, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton, Invesco and Janus Henderson.
Sovereign and public investment institutions, including Singapore's GIC, the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, the Qatar Investment Authority and Norway's Norges Bank Investment Management also queued up, they said.
Indian institutions also had a prominent presence, with major mutual fund houses, including SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, HDFC Mutual Fund, Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund, Nippon India Mutual Fund and Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Company participating.
Insurers and pension investors, including Life Insurance Corporation of India, HDFC Life Insurance, SBI Life Insurance, SBI Pension Funds, HDFC Pension and ICICI Prudential were among those who made offers, sources said.
The breadth of participation spans domestic and overseas institutions with different investment mandates.
Jio Platforms is seeking to raise about Rs 30,213 crore through an initial public offering scheduled to open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. The price band has been set at Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 a share, with the offering comprising up to 27 crore new shares.
The offering is expected to become India's largest IPO, potentially valuing the company at about USD 108 billion at the upper end of the price range. The proceeds are intended in part to support debt repayment at its telecom subsidiary, alongside general corporate purposes, according to the company's offer documents.
Jio Platforms, controlled by billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries, has expanded from its core mobile connectivity business into broadband, digital entertainment, cloud and enterprise services. Its listing will give public-market investors a direct investment route into the business, which has so far operated as a subsidiary of Reliance Industries.
The company had 533.3 million subscribers as of June 2026 and accounted for nearly 60 per cent of India's data traffic, according to reported company figures.
The strong institutional interest could support participation in the broader IPO.
Anchor investors are institutions allotted shares ahead of the public subscription period under the IPO process. Their participation can provide an indication of institutional appetite, although allocations, valuation and subsequent market performance remain separate considerations.

articles.title: UK inflation spikes to almost 3% in July - Trustnet
articles.summary: UK inflation spikes to almost 3% in July  Trustnet
articles.full_text:
UK inflation rose in July to 2.9%, representing a 0.3 percentage-point increase from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, according to the Office for National Statistics. This is the highest annual inflation rate since March, when prices spiked following the outbreak of the war in Iran.
The increase in headline consumer prices is largely tied to utility regulator Ofgem’s 13.5% price cap increase at the beginning of July, which added 0.4 percentage points alone.
Michael Metclafe, head of macro strategy at State Street Markets, said: “With utility prices resetting, the second half of 2026 was always going to be harder on the inflation trend than the first.”
However, not all industries saw a spike. Fuel prices, air fares and restaurants costs all fell. In addition, new prime minister Andy Burnham’s decision to cut VAT from 20% to 5% on families eating out and other cultural services helped to limit inflation.
Kevin Brown, savings expert at Scottish Friendly, pointed out that energy may only be exerting part of the pinch as we move into autumn.
“Expensive fuel and fertiliser are adding pressure to food production and supply chains, while an exceptionally hot summer raises another threat to harvests – as a result, families may continue to feel the inflationary fallout from this at the till as well as through their utility bills,” Brown said.
Meanwhile, Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JP Morgan Personal Investing, agreed that the rebound in UK inflation is a “warning shot” for what could come next.
Gardner said: “We are keeping an eye out to see whether higher global energy prices have a knock-on effect for consumer goods prices, electronics and the wider artificial intelligence build-out.
“This would have an impact on the UK economy and present a challenge for the Bank of England, which is keen to avoid hiking rates. If goods inflation accelerates, then it will become difficult for BofE policymakers to maintain rates at the current level.”
Today’s inflation figures follow updated UK employment figures, which showed continued soft labour market conditions.
Another round of labour market and CPI inflation data will come ahead of the Bank of England’s next meeting on the base rate on 17 September.
Metcalfe expects inflation to accelerate further in August, which will put the Bank under further pressure.
“But as long as inflation remains in the low threes, in line with forecasts, the new more balanced, even dovish, tone of the Bank of England suggests they may escape the year without having to move interest rates at all,” Metcalfe said.
So far, the Bank has held at 3.75%, despite continued pressures and uncertainties generated by the Middle East conflict and turbulent energy prices.

articles.title: China's Financial Street Forum opens today; PBOC's Pan Gongsheng and CSRC's Wu Qing to deliver keynote speeches - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: China's Financial Street Forum opens today; PBOC's Pan Gongsheng and CSRC's Wu Qing to deliver keynote speeches  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
The 2026 Financial Street Forum Annual Conference officially opened in Beijing on October 19. People's Bank of China (PBOC) Governor Pan Gongsheng, Ding Xiangqun, head of China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, and China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) Chairman Wu Qing will attend the opening ceremony and deliver keynote speeches. The market is watching for the latest signals from the heads of China's three main financial regulators on monetary policy, financial regulation and capital market reform in the period ahead.
This year's forum runs from October 19 to October 22 and overlaps closely with major macro events — the release of third-quarter economic data and the loan prime rate (LPR) announcement — positioning it as a key window for gauging policy direction in the fourth quarter.
Macro data and policy signals in dense supply
On the morning of the same day, China's National Bureau of Statistics releases core economic indicators for September, including industrial value-added, fixed-asset investment and retail sales, along with its monthly report on new home prices in 70 major Chinese cities. On October 20, the one-year and five-year-plus LPRs will be published. In September, the one-year LPR stood at 3.0% and the five-year-plus at 3.5%, unchanged for 16 consecutive months.
Before the forum opened, policymakers had already sent several signals. China's State Council Executive Meeting on October 16 heard a report on progress of the "AI+" initiative, stating explicitly that artificial intelligence is a key variable shaping future development. It called for technology innovation to be driven by real-world applications and for the "AI+" initiative to be deepened and expanded in light of China's complete industrial system, rich application scenarios and strong engineering capabilities. The meeting also set out three requirements — shoring up the development foundation, prioritizing enabling applications, and balancing development with security — stressing stronger technological breakthroughs and algorithm innovation, better coordination between computing and power, more high-quality data supply, and closer matching of supply and demand with a focus on the real economy.
Speaking earlier at an emerging markets seminar during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, Pan Gongsheng said China's sustained and stable economic growth and the rapid development of its high-tech industries provide solid support for yuan-denominated assets. He noted that China's stock and bond markets are both the second-largest in the world, with ample liquidity that can effectively meet global investors' diversified allocation needs. In the next stage, the PBOC will further support global investors and issuers in participating in China's financial markets, promote yuan-denominated bonds as widely recognized and used eligible collateral worldwide, and strengthen connectivity of onshore and offshore financial infrastructure.
Technology export controls and industry standards advance in tandem
China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology plan to revise the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, seeking public comment on adding technologies in artificial intelligence, biomedicine and solar power, covering 40 technologies in total. The AI category covers 23 technologies related to large models, intelligent agents, computing clusters and information processing; the biomedicine category covers five technologies related to cell and gene therapy, small nucleic acid drugs and pathogenic microorganisms; and the solar category covers 12 technologies related to polysilicon manufacturing, wafer manufacturing and cell manufacturing. Technologies already in the public domain through open-source release or published academic papers are excluded from the scope, and outbound licensing arrangements that do not involve transfer of ownership qualify for facilitated measures such as automatic licensing.
On industry standards, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, Ministry of Public Security, Ministry of Ecology and Environment and State Administration for Market Regulation convened a symposium with more than 30 major Chinese automakers, requiring them to strengthen testing and validation across the board and to truthfully publicize the usage boundaries and limitations of innovative product designs, and prohibiting false, exaggerated or misleading advertising. The State Administration for Market Regulation also approved and published a mandatory national standard on safety requirements for lithium-ion batteries used in electric motorcycles and electric mopeds, effective July 1, 2027.
Tech leaders launch wave of buybacks as AI supply chain forecasts strong earnings
Ahead of the forum's opening, China's A-share technology sector saw a cluster of buyback announcements. On October 18, Li Jun, chairman of Hygon Information Technology (688041.SS), proposed buying back CNY 500 million to CNY 800 million (approximately $74.8 million to $119.7 million) of the company's shares; Li Jun, chairman and general manager of Sugon (603019.SS), proposed a buyback of CNY 300 million to CNY 500 million (approximately $44.9 million to $74.8 million); Cheng Yuhua, an independent director of Montage Technology (688008.SS), proposed a buyback of CNY 300 million to CNY 500 million (approximately $44.9 million to $74.8 million); and Chen Renxi, chairman of Shengyi Technology (600183.SS), proposed a buyback of CNY 200 million to CNY 300 million (approximately $29.9 million to $44.9 million). All of the repurchased shares are intended for employee stock ownership plans or equity incentives.

Note: Amounts are in yuan.
On earnings, AI supply-chain companies have issued a dense wave of positive third-quarter pre-announcements. ChangXin Technology expects net profit of CNY 131 billion to CNY 132.5 billion (approximately $19.6 billion to $19.8 billion) for the first three quarters, swinging to a profit from a year-earlier loss, mainly on tight DRAM supply and sharply higher prices; Demingli expects net profit of CNY 8.65 billion to CNY 8.95 billion (approximately $1.3 billion) for the first three quarters, also swinging to a profit; Hengtong Optic-Electric expects net profit growth of 151% to 168% year on year for the first three quarters; Shengyi Technology expects growth of 164% to 181%; and Yongtai Technology expects net profit growth of 1,222% for the first three quarters.
In overseas markets, all three major U.S. stock indexes fell last Friday, with the Nasdaq down 2.15%, the S&P 500 down 1.09% and the Dow down 0.34%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 3.83%, its eighth consecutive session of declines. Japanese and South Korean markets opened lower across the board on October 19, with South Korea's KOSPI down 3.17% and Japan's Nikkei 225 down 0.77%.
Market impact
The Financial Street Forum landing in the same period as third-quarter economic data and the LPR quote gives investors a concentrated window to assess policy continuity. Remarks by regulatory chiefs will directly shape market expectations for the liquidity environment and the pace of capital market reform. The revision of the technology export catalogue brings large models and computing clusters into its scope, imposing new compliance requirements on the overseas business plans of relevant companies, though open-source technologies remain outside its reach, preserving room for the industry ecosystem. Concentrated buybacks by tech leaders and upbeat AI supply-chain earnings forecasts are reinforcing each other and lending short-term support to sector sentiment, while the continued correction in overseas semiconductor stocks remains an external variable to watch.

articles.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6897 – Reuters estimate - investingLive
articles.summary: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6897 – Reuters estimate  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- PBOC CNY reference rate setting for the trading session ahead.
The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.
---
The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.
Summary:
- The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.
- China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, allowing the yuan to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the daily midpoint during onshore hours.
- The midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the prior day's close, moves in major currencies, broader international FX conditions and domestic factors such as capital flows and growth momentum, with policymakers retaining discretion over the final number.
- If market pressure pushes the yuan toward either edge of the band, the PBOC can intervene through direct buying or selling of yuan, liquidity adjustments, or guidance via state-owned banks.
- A stronger-than-expected fixing typically signals the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can indicate tolerance for a softer currency or discomfort with the pace of gains.
- For nearly a year the fixing has been set weaker than market estimates, with the gap reaching its widest since February in late August.
- In September the PBOC strengthened the fixing for eight straight sessions, the longest run since 2023, and the midpoint reached its strongest level since February 2023.
- The yuan has pushed to its strongest levels since early 2023 onshore and since mid-2022 offshore, with Goldman Sachs expecting Beijing to remain comfortable with sustained but gradual appreciation.
The People's Bank of China sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT, a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. It has taken on added significance in recent weeks as policymakers have shifted from restraining the yuan's rise to guiding it higher.
China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the yuan is allowed to trade within a band of plus or minus 2% around the central midpoint set each trading day. That midpoint reflects a mix of inputs, including the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies such as the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic considerations like capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The calculation is not purely mechanical, giving policymakers room to use the fixing to guide market expectations.
Once the midpoint is set, onshore USD/CNY trades freely within the allowable range. Should market pressure push the currency toward either edge of that band, the central bank can step in to smooth volatility, whether through direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance channelled through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often read as a policy signal rather than a purely technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected midpoint typically suggests the PBOC is leaning against depreciation, while a weaker fixing can signal tolerance for a softer currency, or unease with how quickly the yuan is rising.
That second reading has dominated for much of the past year. For nearly a year, the central bank set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, a pattern traders and analysts interpreted as an attempt to slow the yuan's appreciation. The gap reached its widest since February in late August, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.
September has brought a clear change of tone. The midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace this month, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the PBOC has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The central bank strengthened the fixing for eight consecutive sessions, the longest streak since 2023, and the midpoint has since reached its strongest level since February 2023. The onshore yuan has traded at its strongest since January 2023, while the offshore rate has reached levels last seen in July 2022. Even so, the fixing is still being set well weaker than market estimates, with one recent midpoint more than 500 pips below a Reuters survey forecast, a reminder that Beijing is allowing appreciation on its own terms rather than stepping aside.
The timing has been linked to diplomacy.
The underlying tension is a familiar one. A firmer yuan supports capital stability and eases import costs, but a rapid rise risks undermining export competitiveness at a moment when China's broader economy continues to show signs of softness. For traders and investors, the gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest windows into how Beijing is weighing that trade-off, and whether the recent green light for gains stays in place once the summit has passed.

articles.title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
articles.summary: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listingAnthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every ...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.
The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.
The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.
The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.
“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.
It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI.
Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.
Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.
It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.
“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”
He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”
Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.
OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government.
Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops lootedFrance has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.
The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.
The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.
“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.
“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”
The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.
Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.
Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.
“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.
The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.
The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.
“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”
The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.
France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.
French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.
Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.
“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

articles.title: Frank Elderson: From climate and nature risks to economic resilience and competitiveness
articles.full_text:
- SPEECH
From climate and nature risks to economic resilience and competitiveness
Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the Green Swan 2026 Conference
Manila, 19 October 2026
Introduction
We are living in a time of profound economic, geopolitical and technological uncertainty. Yet amid all this uncertainty, one thing is clear: climate change and nature degradation will continue to shape our economies and societies, and we will have to deal with the consequences. Climate change and nature degradation are a certainty in an uncertain world. The events of this summer have reminded us of that reality in the most tangible way possible.
For Europe, the summer of 2026 was not simply another warm season. It was the warmest summer ever recorded in Western Europe, marked by severe droughts, devastating wildfires, water scarcity and mounting pressure on ecosystems across the continent.[1] Water levels in major European rivers fell to exceptionally low levels, affecting transport, industry and energy production. At the same time, large areas of land were destroyed by fires and important economic sectors faced disruptions.[2] Europe is warming faster than any other continent at more than twice the global average.[3] The human toll has been severe, with tens of thousands of excess deaths linked to extreme heat recorded during the summer months.[4]
This summer also served as a reminder of how much our economies depend on nature. Water scarcity affected not only households and agriculture, but also manufacturing, transport and energy production. Across Europe, pressure on ecosystems highlighted the fact that healthy forests, soils, rivers, wetlands and oceans are not just environmental assets, but that they provide essential ecosystem services on which economic activity relies every day, and which often go unnoticed until they are put under strain.[5]
Taken together, this summer’s events conveyed a simple but powerful message: climate and nature are not external to our economies. They are embedded within them and, increasingly, they are becoming a macroeconomic concern.
This raises a number of important questions.
How can we strengthen economic resilience in a world of more frequent climate and nature-related shocks?
How do we ensure that, as we pursue the green transition, we also strengthen competitiveness, energy security and long-term prosperity?
And which barriers still stand in the way of the investment needed to make that happen?
Let me address each of these questions in turn.
Climate and nature crises pose a systemic risk
Let me take one step back.
When a drought, flood or wildfire occurs, attention immediately and naturally focuses on the event itself. Taken in isolation, the economic and financial consequences may appear manageable. Yet individual events only tell part of the story. It is a bit like focusing on individual symptoms while ignoring the underlying disease. The more important question is how climate and nature-related shocks add up, interact, reinforce one another and affect economies over time.
In this context, I am reminded of an observation by the economist and author Simon Sharpe.[6] Scientists are trained not to overstate risks. Risk managers are trained not to underestimate them. This points to a trade-off that central bankers and supervisors know well. Faced with uncertainty, we can err in both directions: we can reassure ourselves too readily that a risk will not materialise, or we can raise a false alarm. Reducing the likelihood of one increases the likelihood of the other. Our task is therefore to reduce uncertainty as far as possible through better data and analysis, carefully assess the consequences of getting it wrong, and respond proportionately.[7] We cannot predict the future with certainty, but we can try to understand how risks may evolve, identify vulnerabilities and strengthen resilience.
This is the perspective central banks and supervisors should take when looking at climate and nature crises.
The challenge is compounded by the fact that we are not dealing with a static risk. As temperatures rise and physical hazards intensify, the economic consequences are becoming increasingly dynamic and material.
A growing body of evidence shows that climate-related shocks can leave lasting economic scars. Extreme heat reduces labour productivity. Droughts affect agriculture, industry and transport. Floods damage infrastructure and disrupt production. Investment may be postponed, populations may relocate and economic output can remain below trend for years after major events.[8]
They do not just affect economic activity, but already increasingly affect prices as well. This summer provided fresh examples of this: high temperatures and low water levels disrupted parts of Europe’s energy system and contributed to higher wholesale electricity prices, while extreme weather continues to influence food prices.[9] Climate shocks therefore affect not only growth but also inflation dynamics.
These risks are also inherently cross-border. Food price shocks, supply chain disruptions and migration pressures do not stop at national frontiers.
Nature-related risks operate through similar channels. Recent ECB research suggests that severe water scarcity alone could put up to 24% of the euro area’s economic output at risk. At the same time, a significant share of economic activity and bank lending remains exposed to flood risk.[10]
The lesson is not that a single drought, flood or wildfire will trigger a macroeconomic crisis. As these disasters become more frequent and severe, the lesson is that a hotter planet and nature degradation are increasingly becoming structural drivers of economic and financial outcomes.
This matters directly for central banks and supervisors. Our job description is clear. We are responsible for maintaining price stability and safeguarding banks’ safety, soundness and financial stability. As climate and nature risks increasingly affect productivity, growth, inflation and the resilience of the financial system, taking them into account falls squarely within our mandate. That is why central banks need macroeconomic models and forecasting procedures that reflect the impact of climate change and nature degradation and keep track of the changing structure of the economy.[11]
That is also why forums such as the Green Swan Conference matter. Bringing together central bankers, supervisors, policymakers and academics from around the world is itself an important contribution to resilience. In a world that is facing increasing geopolitical fragmentation and risks, international cooperation and collective efforts remain some of our most essential and valuable tools for advancing our knowledge and addressing shared risks.
Economic resilience requires both adaptation and mitigation
This brings me to my second point.
When discussing the impact of the climate and nature crises, it is important to distinguish clearly between adaptation and mitigation. Adaptation addresses the consequences. Mitigation addresses the causes. We need both.
The reality is that the consequences of climate change and nature degradation will continue to unfold for years to come. Past emissions have already warmed the planet and set in motion changes that cannot simply be reversed overnight. Meanwhile, greenhouse gases continue to accumulate in the atmosphere. We cannot make the risks we already face disappear.[12] That means societies, households, firms and financial institutions need to take pre-emptive action and strengthen their resilience.
We need advanced early-warning systems and infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather. We need better water management, including, flood prevention, energy-efficient cooling and measures against water leakage. We need more resilient energy systems and cities, transport networks and production systems that can continue functioning under more challenging climatic conditions. Adaptation is not optional, it is a necessity for our economies to remain resilient and competitive in the future.
This is not starting from zero. Across Europe, regions and cities are already investing in climate resilience, while initiatives at EU level are supporting adaptation and strengthening our preparedness for water scarcity, floods and wildfires.[13][14] These efforts show what can be done. The challenge now is to accelerate them and bring them to scale.
But adaptation alone is not enough. Without mitigation, the scale of adaptation required becomes progressively larger and more costly. In some places, particularly low-lying coastal areas and small island states, climate change may eventually make adaptation extraordinarily difficult, if not impossible. Mitigation therefore remains essential.
The more effectively we can mitigate climate change and protect nature, the lower the future adaptation costs will be. And the better we adapt, the more resilient our economies will become during the transition. There is no silver bullet. But there is a clear direction of travel.
The transition is a competitiveness strategy
Let me now turn to what I believe is one of the most important debates currently taking place in Europe: the green transition as a central pillar of competitiveness. It is perhaps also an area where policymakers and businesses in many parts of Asia are already providing valuable lessons. And the next panel in today’s conference, on resilience building in the real economy, with business sector representatives from the Philippines, Japan and Europe, couldn’t be timelier in this respect.
In Europe, resilience, energy security, competitiveness and the green transition are still too often perceived as competing objectives. I believe that is the wrong way to think about it. articles.title: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports
articles.summary: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demandRoaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%. Continue readi...
articles.full_text:
Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.
Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.
“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.

articles.title: Christiane Amanpour announces she’s leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.summary: Anchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance MediaChristiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She ...
articles.full_text:
Christiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.
Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She also hosts a show for PBS, Amanpour and Company, that will conclude at the end of this year.
In the statement, Amanpour said she came to the decision to “separate” from the network “after many months of thought and a few sleepless nights”.
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf war, to the horrors of the Bosnian war, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor,” she wrote.
She ended her statement by encouraging her CNN colleagues: “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour, 68, has been open about her ongoing treatment for ovarian cancer, which she was diagnosed with in 2021.
Her decision comes at a notable time for the network, which is now part of a larger media conglomerate called Skydance that is run by David Ellison, with heavy backing from Larry Ellison, his Trump-donor father and Oracle co-founder.
Her exit is not thought to be specifically tied to the network’s new ownership, which is viewed skeptically by some CNN journalists because of its perceived closeness to the Trump administration. But, in her statement, Amanpour seemed to nod to concerns about the network’s future, saying that she “will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism”.
She expanded on that commitment to independence in a taped message to viewers of her CNN International show on Monday afternoon.
“You know that I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” she said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides – political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field.”
In his own memo, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson, who announced earlier this month that he will be remaining with the merged company, thanked Amanpour “for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship”.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Amanpour said she will continue hosting her podcast, The Ex Files and that she “[looks] forward to interesting new projects down the line”.
